#7984. Discovery Sanctions Recommended in "Are You a Jew? … Are You a Zionist?" Case

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The factual allegations, from a Sept. 2025 decision in the case by Judge Susan Illston (N.D. Cal.) (the case is Radice v. Jerusalem Boxing Club, LLC consolidated with the federal government's U.S. v. Harara):

The Jerusalem Coffee House [which Harara owns] is a business establishment open to the general public. The coffee house is located on the premises of the East Bay Community Space, "which regularly hosts events that are open to the general public for exhibition or entertainment …."

According to the complaint, on June 10, 2024, Michael Radice—who is Jewish—went to the East Bay Community Space "for the purpose of viewing the establishment for a fundraising event for his organization." Radice was wearing a dark blue baseball cap with a light blue Star of David and white Hebrew lettering. As he approached the community space from the side where the coffee house is located, a man sitting at a table in front of the coffee house asked, "Are you a Jew?" Radice answered in the affirmative. The man then asked, "Are you a Zionist?" Radice declined to respond.

The complaint alleges that "[t]he man then began shouting numerous accusations at Mr. Radice, including that he was complicit in Israel's military actions in the Gaza Strip following the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks and guilty of 'killing children.'" As Radice began to walk away, the man stood up and asked, "Where are you going?" The complaint alleges, "Mr. Radice saw another man, whom he later learned was Harara, walk out of the coffee house and speak to the man, and the two went inside." …

And now from Judge Thomas Hixson's Report and Recommendation yesterday:

There is no dispute that Defendant Abdulrahim Harara violated at least six discovery orders. Motion at 4-7 ("Harara has flouted at least six discovery orders," and enumerating the violations); Opp. at 7 ("But the question on this motion is not whether any order was violated; it is whether the record as a whole shows the kind of deliberate, deceptive obstruction that makes a fair trial impossible and justifies ending the case without one.")….

The real issue is what remedy the Court should impose for the serial violations of its discovery orders. The impact of Harara's conduct basically falls into three buckets: documents were produced late that should have been produced earlier; some document productions are incomplete; and there has been a wholesale failure to produce email. But having reviewed the voluminous evidence submitted in support of Radice's motion for sanctions, the Court thinks truth is available to the parties, and they should go ahead and have a trial on the existing record.

Harara's biggest failure in discovery is the nonproduction of email, and he does not have a good excuse. In many cases the total failure to produce email would justify terminating sanctions or at least adverse inference instructions.

But the Court is skeptical that this is such a case. The relevant events are alleged in-person refusals to serve Radice and another individual because they are Jewish. In other words, the relevant events did not occur by email. Before email existed, public accommodation discrimination claims like this were tried the old fashioned way: The participants in the alleged events testified, and the trier of fact decided who to believe. That option is still available here.

Email is still relevant, of course, because it could contain statements about what happened, or have evidence of the defendant's allegedly prejudicial intent. But here a lot of that type of evidence was produced in the form of Harara's text messages and social media feeds and other electronic records. These include a statement that seems to be by Harara that seems to say he throws pennies on the ground when Jews walk by; the coffee shop menu and outdoor signage with inverted red triangles, which Radice alleges is a symbol used by Hamas to mark Israeli targets in propaganda videos; the apparent introduction on the one year anniversary of the October 7 attack of a juice item named for a mastermind of the attack; a video of Harara telling a Jewish customer to leave because he had "a violent hat," referring to the Star of David on the hat; and a repost by Harara to his X account bearing the "Bay Area" screen name of a November 2, 2024 post calling that same Jewish customer "a genocidal, bottom dwelling Zionist scum" who "should be kicked out of every public establishment not just Palestinian owned ones!" There are also text messages that replicate the kind of thing a plaintiff would dream of finding in a defendant's emails—and certainly at trial Radice and the United States will argue these texts are strong evidence of liability.

Radice is certainly of the view that he has uncovered good evidence, even if it was produced later than it should have been, and even though it does not include email. See Motion at 15 ("The 6134 Bates-labeled pages and 2474 native files that Harara produced on or after August 7 include inflammatory documents that Harara willfully withheld until after discovery closed."); id. ("For example, a January 3, 2025 JCH Instagram post shows JCH advertising for sale a t-shirt featuring the Jerusalem Coffee House name ringed by flags with the emblem of Hamas, a designated terrorist organization dedicated to violence against Jews and Israelis."); id. ("His Instagram direct-messages contain both antisemitic tropes and antisemitic slurs.").

With all this evidence, can it really be said that Harara's failings in discovery have prejudiced Plaintiffs to such an extent that a meaningful and fair trial is no longer possible? That adverse inferences are needed because there is not enough evidence for the trier of fact to reliably draw conclusions about what happened?

No. These cases are about whether a coffee shop committed discrimination, and Harara has produced enough documents that Radice and the United States have what they need to go to trial. Even with the nonproduction of email, it is not true that discovery failed or that truth cannot be ascertained. The public policy in favor of deciding cases on the merits applies here.

Accordingly, the Court RECOMMENDS that the district judge DENY the request for terminating sanctions because there's just no need or basis for it. The Court DENIES the request for adverse inferences because it is essentially a request for a directed verdict. Each side should put on their case at trial, and truth should be determined in the normal way. There is no reason for the Court to stack the deck.

But that doesn't mean Harara escapes sanctions. He needs to pay for what he did. His serial violations of Court orders significantly drove up Radice's cost of litigating [the case]. Radice requests $166,500.50 against all Defendants. The entity Defendants have been in default during the period of time when Harara violated the Court orders, so are not the cause of Radice's increased legal expenses, and therefore will not be sanctioned.

Plaintiff's counsel's rates are reasonable. However, both the Benesch and ADL attorneys seek fees for work that preceded the violations of the Court orders, a problem that requires deducting about a third of the Benesch time and about a fifth of the ADL's time. That brings the total down to $118,000. In addition, even though Harara violated multiple discovery orders, it is also true that Plaintiff's counsel litigated [the case] with excessive ferocity. At times it seemed they were not just litigating a discrimination case but were out to destroy Harara. As a result their fees were excessive. The Court estimates that about half of the fees Radice incurred during the time when Harara was violating the discovery orders was due to the violations and the other half was for work that would have needed to be done anyway or that should not have been done at all because it was excessive. Accordingly, the Court SANCTIONS Harara in the amount of $59,000 and ORDERS him to pay that amount to Radice within 30 days.

In his opposition, Harara proposes some remedial measures. However, the Court will not adopt any of them. The proposal to remedy the lack of email production presupposes that Harara will have a lawyer to represent him. Opp. at 16 ("The full inbox Mr. Harara exported on September 3, 2026 will be reviewed by counsel, consistent with the Court's ruling that counsel rather than Mr. Harara conduct that review. That counsel will be either counsel Mr. Harara retains or volunteer limited-scope counsel appointed through the Court's Federal Pro Bono Project under General Order 25, to which Mr. Harara respectfully requests referral. Since his counsel withdrew, Mr. Harara has contacted lawyers and legal organizations and has not found a lawyer who will take his case."). However, Harara's inability to work cooperatively with two sets of counsel means this is an unrealistic proposal. And if no lawyer represents him, Harara's proposal contains no particular deadline by which emails would be produced. Opp. at 16 ("If counsel has not been retained or appointed within 30 days of the Court's order, Mr. Harara will file a status report every 14 days thereafter. In all events, the production under this paragraph will be complete within 90 days of the Court's order; if it is not, Mr. Harara will show cause why not, and the Court may then impose such further measures as it finds appropriate after notice and an opportunity to be heard.").

Harara's proposal to serve further interrogatory responses is highly unlikely to achieve anything. And there is no need for a further deposition of him; Plaintiffs' counsel can cross-examine him at trial….

NEXT: 10-Year "Harassment"/"Stalking" Sentence for Repeatedly Criticizing Police Detective Violated First Amendment, Amicus Brief Argues

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7983. The Best Circular Saws of 2026, Tested by Experts

By Glenda Taylor, Additional research provided by Tom Scalisi

Published Oct 27, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Anyone who’s worked on a construction site or been part of their home’s renovation knows how versatile circular saws are. When it comes to breaking down a sheet of plywood and making quick, repetitive cuts on a stack of framing lumber, it’s the best tool for the job. Still, with the abundance of saw brands, power options, and features available, choosing the right one can be challenging. That’s why we tested 10 top models to see which will push your project along and which might hold you back.

To help us select the models we feel confident recommending, we also reached out to a home improvement expert to get his take on how to choose one of these powerful tools. Based on his insights and our hands-on tests, we chose the Makita XSH06PT 36V Brushless 7¼” Circular Saw Kit as our favorite circular saw for its quality contraction and user-friendly operation.

The results of our tests on the Makita XSH06PT and the rest of the saws is below, alongside a quick peek at a product that wasn’t reliable enough to make our list. After pushing these tools to their limits cutting timbers, particle-strand lumber (PSL), plywood, and dimensional lumber, we can accurately say the following lineup represents a solid selection of the best circular saws on the market.

Bottom line: Experts tested top circular saws, with Makita XSH06PT leading for quality and ease of use, while other models offer budget and specialized options.

Choosing a circular saw doesn’t have to be confusing. Review the results of our hands-on tests as well as each tool’s pros and cons to help you select the model that’s right for your next project.

The 36-volt cordless Makita circular saw takes top honors in our lineup of the best circular saws for several reasons. First, its base (or “shoe”) and its retractable blade guard are made from magnesium, which offers more durability than steel or aluminum at a lighter weight. It’s also powerful, has a long list of easy-to-use features, and offers an impressive cutting capacity.

We tested the Makita by making straight and bevel cuts of various depths on plywood and dimensional lumber. It powered through smoothly with no torque loss, even after the battery indicators showed less than half a charge. We made repeated cuts over an hour, and the Makita’s motor and housing never heated up.

We also liked that this battery-powered circular saw has a handy quick-change angle adjustment, allowing cuts up to 56 degrees with positive stops at standard angles of 22½, 45, and 56 degrees. Its depth is easy to adjust up to 2⅝ inches, making this tool great for quick-moving projects where you don’t want to stop and use a wrench to change settings. While this handheld circular saw also has a sawdust discharge nozzle for wet/dry vacuum hose connect, we noticed quite a bit of sawdust still escaped from around the blade guard, making this feature of the saw the only one we don’t totally endorse.

Read our full review: Makita XSH06PT 36V Brushless 7¼” Circular Saw Kit

What our tester says: “If I could only choose one circular saw for most nonshop situations—either a corded 7¼-inch model or the Makita XSH06PT—I’d choose the Makita. It offers as much cutting power as most corded saws, and purchasing a couple of extra lithium-ion batteries eliminates any downtime. Corded models are great when you’re in a shop with plenty of outlets, but this Makita is excellent when portability matters.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Makita 36V circular saw at Amazon or The Home Depot.

Not everyone needs all of the features of a top-of-the-line cordless saw or the heavy-duty capability of a timber-framing model. For DIY projects that include an occasional small framing job or breaking down plywood sheets—especially when saving money is a priority—the affordable Greenworks 7¼-Inch circular saw might be the right choice.

We’ve tested plenty of tools from many manufacturers, but this is the first Greenworks power tool we tried, and we were pleasantly surprised. Despite its affordable price, this circular saw made repeated straight and bevel cuts in plywood and dimensional lumber over an hour of solid testing without heating up on us or losing power. It tops out at 4,500 RPM, which is slightly less speed than some of the other saws we tested, but it will be sufficient for cutting the types of wood most DIYers will need to cut.

The CR24L00K features quick adjustments for both angle cutting (up to 45 degrees) and cutting depth (up to 2½ inches), and we found it simple to adjust both. The base shoe is made from stamped metal, which is to be expected at this price point, but we were disappointed that the blade guard is plastic—it really should be metal. The blade guard didn’t break during our tests, but it’s a weak point in the tool’s design.

Get the Greenworks circular saw at Amazon.

For part-time DIYers or smaller-framed users, Makita’s 18V LXT cordless 5⅜-inch circular saw’s small size and minimal weight make it an attractive, portable option. This lightweight circular saw weighs just 6 pounds, allowing DIYers of any size and skill level to wield it. It’s well suited to overhead cutting where it isn’t easy to wield a heavier circular saw.

Despite its minimal size and small blade, this Makita cordless circular saw has a depth of cut of up to 2 inches, offering more than enough capacity for cutting dimensional lumber. Its 3,600-RPM top speed should be capable of handling most projects, though the speed is less than some competitive models. The base bevels up to 50 degrees to allow users to make angled cuts.

Although small, we found that this portable circular saw packs quite a punch. It easily powered through straight and angled cuts in plywood and dimensional lumber. While the dual support knob is a little on the small side, we were able to use it to keep the saw stable while cutting. Most pros will probably forgo the dual support and use this model as a one-handed saw.

Get the Makita 18V circular saw at Amazon.

Those seeking a pro-level circular saw for DIY jobs should consider this Skil PWR CORE model. While it looks like a worm-drive saw because of its length and heft, it’s actually a sidewinder with its motor located next to the blade rather than behind it. Upon inspection, we realized the additional length comes from the positioning of the double-battery case, which sits to the rear of the motor.

In our tests, controlling the saw when cutting dense wood and larger pieces of dimensional lumber was made easy by grasping the rear handle and the dual stabilizer bar at the front. The saw’s two 20-volt, 5Ah batteries, provide more than enough power to make repetitive straight and angled cuts on plywood and dimensional lumber. Since it’s billed as a heavy-duty model, we also tested the saw on laminated veneer lumber (LVL), which is very dense and difficult to cut, and it cut through without bogging down.

We like this saw’s deeper-than-average cutting depth of 2 9/16 inches and its up to 53-degree-angle cutting capacity. What we don’t like is having to press a second lever to adjust the blade angle beyond 53 degrees, as it feels uncomfortable and seems unnecessary. We also would prefer a magnesium base shoe to the aluminum one, but we appreciate how the elongated shoe style helps stabilize the saw on deep cuts.

What our tester says: “This saw is well designed, ergonomic, and suitable for heavy-duty DIY use. It’s the Skil model we feel bridges the gap between a standard consumer and a pro tool.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Skil PWR CORE circular saw at Ace Hardware.

Getting the hang of using a circular saw can be challenging, but operating a circular saw with laser guidance makes the process much easier. This Skil electric circular saw features a single-beam laser that allows users to maintain consistent passes on cutlines, taking some of the learning curve out of straight cuts. While we’ve found that some laser guides are dim or don’t extend more than a few inches, the laser on the Skil saw is a notable exception. Even outdoors on a mostly sunny day, it was visible on our cutting material for more than 2 feet.

In addition to its laser beam, this corded circular saw also boasts a 5,300-RPM top speed from its 15-amp motor, offering plenty of power and capability. It cuts angles up to 51 degrees and comes with a positive stop at 45 degrees—the angle used most often when cutting miters. Adjusting both angle and depth is simple via levers, and the tool comes with a maximum cutting depth of 2.4357 inches.

While we deem this saw a good choice for making straight and angled cuts on plywood and dimensional lumber, it’s not for heavy-duty sawing. The motor got pretty warm to the touch after about 45 minutes of use, which told us that we were pushing it further than it was designed to go. The saw also has several plastic components, which help keep the price down but make it better for novice DIYers needing a saw for small projects.

Get the Skil corded circular saw at Amazon, Ace Hardware, Lowe’s, or Walmart.

Though this large circular saw from Skil weighs a hefty 16.45 pounds, has a substantial 10¼-inch blade, and operates at a respectable 4,700 RPM—it’s neither the biggest nor the fastest model on our list. Still, it produces enough torque to keep spinning through thick and dense timbers associated with post-and-beam and timber framing. During testing, we used it to make a variety of straight and angled cuts on dimensional lumber and an LVL, and it didn’t heat up at all.

As with most of today’s worm-drive saws, this model is corded because its size and torque demand more power than most lithium-ion batteries can produce. It performed flawlessly when we used it to bevel the edge of a large 8-foot-long 12-inch by 12-inch Hem-Fir beam, and it has an enviable cutting depth of 3 11/16 inches. It cuts angles up to 51 degrees, and both the blade angle and depth are easy to adjust via levers. Over our testing period, our arms and shoulders did get a bit tired from the weight of this saw, making this model a bit much for occasional-use DIYers. If you need to cut sizable dimensional lumber or timbers, however, this is the machine for you.

Get the Skil Worm Drive circular saw at Amazon or Lowe’s.

We’ve purchased “tool-only” power tools in the past, only to find we had to pay as much or more to then buy a compatible battery and charger. The Bosch Profactor circular saw gets around that issue by including the brushless circular saw, battery, charger, and a heavy-duty canvas bag as a complete kit.

But the Bosch isn’t just about a certain quantity of pieces, it’s also a quality tool that cuts up to 50-degree angles and 2½-inch depths. It features easy-to-change adjustments, and though its base shoe and blade guard are aluminum, it’s a well-built saw that, at 12 pounds, weighs slightly more than some of the similar 7¼-inch models we tested.

We made near-constant straight and angled cuts through dimensional lumber and plywood for over an hour, and this saw didn’t come close to overheating. An interesting aspect of this model is that its blade is on the left, whereas the blades on most 7¼-inch circular saws are on the right. While this took a little getting used to, we didn’t feel it was a downside—the saw can be used easily by a right-handed or left-handed user.

We had high hopes for the Black+Decker 20-Volt Compact Circular Saw, but it didn’t quite live up to our standards. Unfortunately, this little 5½-inch saw couldn’t muster enough power to make a ½-inch-deep cut in plywood, even though its 20-volt 1.5Ah lithium-ion battery should have been sufficient for such a shallow cut.

Putting together a list of good circular saws was more fun than work—after all, we have years of experience with these tools. Drawing on our expertise, we whittled our testing list down from over 25 to just 10 carefully selected models. We then used our selected saws to make straight and angled cuts in a variety of materials for a solid hour.

When cutting, we only used manufacturer-suggested materials for each model, not attempting to cut LVLs, which are very dense and difficult to cut, with compact circular saws that are not made to withstand that type of cutting. Likewise, we didn’t bother cutting plywood with worm-drive saws, which are explicitly designed to cut denser, thicker materials like timbers.

We monitored each saw to see whether it got hot during use, how easy/challenging it was to adjust blade angle and cutting depth, and if it lived up to the manufacturer’s depth claims. We scored each machine based on a rubric and used our results to determine each tool’s best use.

Motor alignment, run speed, amperages, and blade types are all essential aspects of a circular saw, so here’s a quick primer on all the types of circular saws and necessary considerations to get your search started.

As with any type of saw, corded circular saws tie the user to the power source (i.e., an electric socket), whereas battery-operated models can be used anywhere. On professional job sites, cordless circular saws were once shunned in favor of corded models, but with the recent improvements in lithium-ion batteries, this is changing.

Today’s battery-operated cordless circular saws have much more power and far longer battery life than early models. Much of this improvement is due to the adoption of brushless motors (the latest, most efficient, maintenance-free technology) and higher-quality lithium-ion batteries, though the most powerful models are still corded.

According to Ron Shimek, President of Mr. Handyman, a Neighborly company, “A corded saw is the best option for consistent power and performance. Corded saws typically offer superior power and cutting capacity, especially for demanding tasks like ripping through thick lumber.” He points out, however, that cordless options are ideal for outdoor or remote jobs, so you may need different tools for different circumstances.

Sidewinder and worm drive refer to motor alignment and position on a circular saw. A sidewinder model’s motor is installed in line with the blade, enabling it to run at high speeds in a compact footprint.

A worm-drive circular saw has a motor in the rear of the saw and uses a set of worm gears (so-called because of their spiraling worm shape) by the blade. Worm-drive saws, which are usually longer, larger, and heavier than sidewinders, tend to reduce speed but increase torque (force). They also require oil to lubricate the gears, so users should check their oil level daily.

For speed, size, and ease of maintenance, a sidewinder model is the way to go. For power and torque, worm-drive saws reign supreme.

Amperage is the amount of electrical power a motor can withstand without its inner components failing. In the past, electric motors were weaker and not as capable, so amperage (amp) was an important specification to tout. Nearly all modern corded circular saws feature 15-amp motors.

A saw’s speed, however, can be a consideration since the faster the blade spins, the quicker it can cut through a material. But speeds tend to be relative because a 15-amp motor can spin a 7¼-inch blade faster than a 10¼-inch blade. Generally speaking, when it comes to 7¼-inch saws, speeds between 4,000 and 5,500 revolutions per minute (RPM) are common and should be adequate for fast, accurate results. Worm drives may offer slightly lower speeds but come with more torque (spinning force), so while they may cut more slowly, they won’t overheat or bog down during big cutting jobs.

Keep in mind that blade speed has very little to do with the density of material a saw can cut. This is largely dependent on the blade type and quality, and you may need to change a circular saw blade to a higher-quality version to cut denser substances.

One noticeable difference among circular saw models is the size of their blades, as each uses a specific-size blade. The average pro or DIYer can get most framing and construction jobs done with a 7¼-inch model. Compact saws might feature blades in the 5⅜-inch range, while large saw blades can be 10¼ inches or more.

Popular types of circular saw blades include all-purpose, framing, finish, and plywood blades. The tooth count (the number of teeth around a blade) determines which projects a blade works best for. The lower the tooth count, the rougher the cut will be, making these blades suitable for framing or demolition. Higher-count blades should be used for cabinetmaking, plywood, and finish work.

Pro Tip: Circular saws cut on the “upswing,” meaning the cutting half of the blade (the part under the shoe) spins toward the front of the saw. This will inevitably cause tiny slivers of wood to “tear out” of the wood—particularly when cutting plywood—creating noticeably rough edges that detract from the quality of work. To minimize this, lay a piece of painter’s tape over the cutline to hold these fibers in place. It’s also possible to cut wood face down to eliminate tear-out concerns on the face of the wood. For more tips, see our guide on how to use a circular saw.

The base plate that rides on the workpiece is known as a shoe, which will generally be made of one of three materials:

Certain materials, such as plywood and other sheet goods, require a shallow blade depth, while others (framing applications, 4×4 posts, etc.) demand the full depth a saw can muster. For true versatility, a circular saw should allow the user to make quick and accurate depth adjustments.

Almost all models feature levers or knobs to adjust the blade angle, known as the “bevel.” Knobs tend to be more accurate at dialing in the perfect angle, although they’re a bit of a hassle to loosen and tighten when wearing work gloves.

The most important consideration when it comes to blade angle adjustment is an easily accessible level or knob. Some manufacturers put these knobs in an inconvenient place—for instance, the rear of the saw between the handle and blade guard—but an angle-adjustment knob in front of the motor where it’s easy to access is the most thoughtful design.

Manufacturers build safety features into their machines to combat the dangers inherent to circular saws. One helpful safety feature is an electric brake, which stops circular saw blades almost immediately after the user releases the trigger. Older models would allow the blade to come to a stop on its own, which could result in a spinning blade coming into contact with something unintended.

Built-in LED lights and spring-loaded blade guards also offer significant safety measures. Work lights illuminate the workpiece, allowing the user to see the cutline and any debris or impending mistakes they should avoid. Retractable guards cover the blade as soon as the blade is removed from the workpiece, helping to minimize dangers.

Safety is also the responsibility of the user, so be sure to wear eye and ear protection when using a circular saw, miter saw, track saw, or table saw.

Some of the best circular saws offer additional features that make the job easier and faster. For instance, some models have dust-collection ports and detachable collection bags to help minimize the amount of sawdust on the cutline. Depending on the kit, cordless saws might come with extra batteries.

Another helpful feature that manufacturers offer with their saws is a built-in rafter hook. These hooks swivel out of the saw, allowing the user to hang them from a rafter, ladder, sawhorse, or another sturdy ledge. Builders have been attaching hooks to their saws for years, and manufacturers are now catching on.

The most common use for a circular saw is cutting framing lumber to length. However, it can also trim deck boards, cut plywood sheets into cabinet panels, cut metal, and even trim plastic.

Circular saws can cut straight lines, make cuts with beveled angles, and even create a series of thin, shallow cuts known as dadoes or rabbets. These kinds of cuts are achievable on both hard and soft materials including pressure-treated or hard wood.

The Makita 36V circular saw is one of the best circular saws for a variety of home projects, including those DIYers are most likely to tackle.

The best way to keep a circular saw straight is to clamp a straight edge to the workpiece and run the base against it. Another method is to place a small clamp on the front of the base to act as a guide. Ron Shimek, President of Mr. Handyman, a Neighborly company, also points out that “features like laser guides, beveling capabilities, and precise blade depth adjustment contribute to accurate cuts” and clean, straight lines.

Kickback can occur for a few reasons:Don’t start the saw with the blade against the workpiece. Allow the blade to get up to speed before pushing it through the workpiece.Semi-cut workpieces tend to droop, and this droop can cause sideways friction on the blade, pinching it in place. Support the workpiece until the cut is complete.Hitting a knot in the wood can cause kickback because knots are harder than the rest of the wood. Look for knots when measuring the wood, and try to avoid cutting through them.

Glenda Taylor is a product tester and writer specializing in the construction, remodeling, and real estate industries. She and her husband own a general contracting company, and Taylor is experienced in both residential and commercial building applications. She tests a wide range of power tools as well as other home improvement, household, and lawn-and-garden products.

Additional research provided by Tom Scalisi.

#7982. Diagnosing a Ghost – The Mysterious Feline Disease Whose Signs Appear & Disappear

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Waxing and waning signs, vague symptoms that come and go. A cat that is on deathâs door one moment, running around the next. Detecting illness in cats can be difficult enough, but when the body starts attacking itself, diagnosis becomes even more of a challenge.

In an autoimmune disease, a catâs immune system malfunctions and begins attacking the body it is meant to protect. Fortunately, autoimmune disease is relatively uncommon in cats, but it can be serious and difficult to diagnose and treat. Because the signs tend to be vague and can come and go, they are easy to overlook, which makes it worth knowing what to watch for and when to involve a vet.

A healthy immune system protects the body from germs such as viruses and bacteria by sending out specialized cells to locate and destroy them. It also helps clear away damaged or diseased cells. These immune cells use protein signals on the surface of the bodyâs own cells to recognize them as safe. In autoimmune disease, a signaling error causes the immune system to treat the catâs own cells as a threat, and healthy, working tissue gets attacked and destroyed.

Cats can develop these problems much as people do. They can affect any part of the body, including the internal organs, blood, and skin, and there are many different types. Some can be life-threatening, weakening the bodyâs natural defenses while also damaging healthy tissue.

The part of the body under attack determines which signs appear, so the picture varies dramatically from one cat to the next. Signs are often general and not immediately linked to an autoimmune problem. Possible signs include lethargy, weakness, decreased appetite, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, and other changes to the feces. Other signs include pale gums, unexplained bleeding, bruising, a high temperature, a faster heart rate, rapid breathing, and tiring easily during play. Limping, swollen joints, sores on the skin, a poor coat, increased thirst, increased urination, and collapse are also on the list.

Many of these signs come and go. A cat may seem completely fine one day and be struggling the next. Any of these signs are a reason to contact a vet promptly, since starting investigations early makes a real difference.

The problem starts with the catâs own immune system, which is part of what makes it so hard to manage. The exact triggers are not fully understood, and more research is needed. An immune-mediated condition can be triggered when the immune system is stimulated. Viral infections, vaccination, medications, inherited conditions, and hormones have all been linked to autoimmune disease. Where things get tricky is that the incident that triggered the disease is not usually the cause of the disease. That means that the same type of autoimmune disease can be triggered by different things in different individuals.

Some of these conditions can be passed down, and other possible contributors include poor nutrition, toxins, cancer, and stress. A cat diagnosed with an autoimmune disease considered hereditary should not be bred under any circumstances.

Diagnosis is often a process of elimination. More common causes of the same signs are investigated and ruled out first, which can mean lots of tests. A vet will start with a full physical exam and a detailed history, then choose tests to fit the signs. These may include blood and urine tests, X-rays, or an ultrasound scan. Samples may also be taken from wounds, rashes, or other affected areas. Prompt diagnosis is important for effective management.

Treatment depends on the type of autoimmune disease, what part of the body is affected, and what is behind it, so it varies greatly. The usual approach is medication that calms the immune system so it stops attacking the body, most often corticosteroids like prednisone or dexamethasone. A large starting dose is often given, and once the signs settle down, the dose is lowered gradually.

Sometimes, stronger immunosuppressive drugs are also used. Some of them are also used in cancer treatment, and the side effects tend to be more severe. The trouble with treating an immune-mediated disease is that we are using medication to suppress the immune system, and that leaves the patient more susceptible to infection and other diseases.

Even more challenging when treating feline autoimmune disease is that some of the medications used to treat dogs or humans are toxic to cats.

Supportive care matters just as much. Pain relief is often needed, but many commonly prescribed anti-inflammatory painkillers cannot be given alongside steroids. Stronger painkillers like opioids or gabapentin may be used to manage severe pain, and these come with their own side effects. Antibiotics may also be prescribed, either prophylactically if extremely high doses of immunosuppressive medications are being used, or if secondary infections develop.

For cats with immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA), where the immune system is attacking and destroying red blood cells, or immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (IMTP) where platelets are being destroyed, blood or plasma transfusions may be needed to save a catâs life.

Lifestyle changes can help too. A cat with painful, swollen joints, for example, benefits from losing weight if overweight, and lower sides on litter trays and softer beds make life more comfortable. Each case is assessed individually.

One of the more common autoimmune diseases in cats is known as Eosinophilic Granuloma Complex, a group of idiopathic conditions that are currently quite poorly understood. The exact cause of the disease is unknown; however, parasites, allergies, and genetic factors have been identified as likely triggers.

There are three main clinical presentations of eosinophilic granuloma complex:

Ulcerative: Also known as indolent ulcers or rodent ulcers, this form of eosinophilic granuloma complex usually presents with a sore on the cat's mouth. It is typically seen on the upper lip. They are normally red in color and do not appear to cause your cat any pain or irritation.

Plaque-forming: often found on the stomach and on the inside of the hind legs. The lesions are often itchy and red and often become infected, which complicates matters.

Granuloma forming: usually presents as raised pink or yellow nodules that can be located anywhere on your cat.

Another more common feline immune-mediated disease is called pemphigus foliaceus. It affects the skin, causing scabs, crusts, and sores around the eyes and ears, on the paws, and in the groin area. When it develops on the paws, the nail beds can be affected as well.

There is no cure for autoimmune disease, but effective treatment and management can control the signs, greatly improve quality of life, and allow most cats to live fairly comfortably. These conditions can be debilitating and life-threatening, yet it is often possible to manage them well enough for cats to lead relatively normal lives. Because the signs overlap with so many other conditions, a vet visit at the first sign that something is wrong is the surest way to get answers early.

#7981. Trick or Treat? These Halloween Hazards Can Be Hellish For Dogs

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Halloween packs a steady stream of costumed strangers and bowls of candy into a single evening, and for dogs that combination carries more hazards than most people expect. Most of the risks are easy to avoid with a little planning, and several of them start well before the first trick-or-treater arrives at the door. These precautions help keep dogs out of trouble while the rest of the household enjoys Halloween.

Halloween candy can be dangerous for dogs, and the wrappers create an additional hazard. Certain ingredients in sweets, including chocolate and xylitol, can be toxic to dogs, while swallowed wrappers can cause choking or digestive problems.

Keeping candy in a closed container at home is a good starting point, but the risk doesn't end at the front door. Keeping a close eye on what a dog sniffs or picks up can help prevent an unwanted snack from turning into a veterinary emergency.

Costumes for dogs can be adorable and hilarious, but only if the dog agrees. Not every dog feels happy playing dress-up, so itâs important to pay attention to how they respond.

A costume should fit comfortably without restricting movement or creating opportunities for the dog to become tangled. An outfit that fit last year may now be too tight, while one bought for a puppy to grow into could be awkward or unsafe in the meantime.

Before heading out or welcoming visitors, check that the costume fits properly and your pup can walk comfortably in it.

A Halloween costume can look adorable on a dog, but wearing one safely requires supervision. Some dogs become fascinated by their outfits and start chewing at loose fabric or accessories, potentially creating a choking hazard.

There's no reason every dog has to avoid costumes, provided the outfit is comfortable and the dog tolerates wearing it. But if the dog needs to be left alone, take the costume off. It's a simple precaution that reduces the chance of an otherwise harmless outfit causing trouble.

Halloween can be overwhelming for dogs that struggle with noise, unfamiliar people, or constant activity. Trick-or-treaters arrive throughout the evening, and costumes can make even familiar surroundings feel different.

A dog that becomes overexcited or anxious may benefit from having somewhere quiet to retreat. A separate room with a comfortable bed, fresh water, and familiar toys can provide a welcome break from the commotion.

Make sure visitors understand that the dog shouldn't be disturbed if it chooses to settle somewhere away from the activity.

Jack-o'-lanterns, lights, and other Halloween decorations can make a home feel festive, but curious dogs may see them as things to investigate or chew. Keep decorations out of reach, particularly anything that could be harmful if swallowed.

Real candles inside pumpkins also pose a risk if a dog knocks one over. Battery-operated alternatives are a safer choice, especially in areas where pets can wander freely.

Glow sticks and glowing bracelets help make children more visible during evening trick-or-treating, but their bright colors and flexible shapes can also attract a dog's attention.

The liquid inside can cause irritation and may be harmful if swallowed. A dog that bites through a glow stick could end up ingesting the contents, so these items should be kept well away from curious mouths.

Check the ground during walks, too, particularly on Halloween night when discarded glow sticks and bracelets may be lying around. If a dog chews or swallows one, contact a vet for advice.

Handing out candy can mean opening the front door dozens of times in a single evening. For a dog that's curious, excitable, or easily frightened, those repeated opportunities can make an escape more likely.

Closing the door between visitors helps prevent a dog from slipping outside unnoticed. Another option is to step outside to greet trick-or-treaters and close the door behind you.

Keeping the dog in a separate room during busy periods adds another layer of protection. It also reduces the chance of a dog becoming startled by costumed visitors appearing at the entrance.

An identification tag and microchip are always a good idea, but they become particularly important on a night when doors are opening frequently, and unusual sights may startle a dog.

If a dog escapes, an ID tag with current contact details gives whoever finds it a straightforward way to get in touch. A microchip provides another means of identifying the dog and helping it return home.

Check that the dog's tag is attached securely and that the contact information associated with its microchip is up to date. These small steps can make a significant difference if a dog gets loose.

Halloween can be stressful and dangerous for dogs, but it doesnât have to be. Keeping candy secured, choosing comfortable costumes, providing a quiet retreat, and making sure the front door stays closed can prevent many of the problems associated with the holiday.

It's also worth remembering that dogs may react unpredictably to unfamiliar costumes and unusual activity, even if they're normally relaxed around visitors. Staying attentive from the first doorbell to the last helps keep the evening enjoyable for everyone, including the four-legged members of the household.

#7980. Small, Inexpensive Projects That Will Transform Your Bathroom

Updated Oct 27, 2026 11:29 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Transforming your bathroom doesn’t have to require a massive budget or a total demolition and new layout to achieve a high-end feel. In fact, the National Kitchen & Bath Association 2026 Bath Trends Report notes that 64 percent of designers identify homeowners opting for smaller refreshes over large-scale renovations as a major emerging trend. By focusing on high-impact, affordable updates, you can revitalize your bathroom in a single weekend. This guide covers five simple, small bathroom projects that deliver professional results in no time.

Decluttering and finding effective storage solutions in your bathroom can not only make it look more appealing but will also create a more relaxing environment. It naturally feels far more refined and purposeful to have a more open surface, says Alan Solis, CEO of Solis Painting in Springfield, New Jersey. “By clearing countertops, taking unused products out of the equation, and reducing what is on display, you are instantly making it feel cleaner and more spacious,” explains Solis. Folding towels neatly and displaying them intentionally on a towel bar is another example of a small, free way to shift the mood of the room.

Choosing smart storage is another way to improve the look and feel of a bathroom. Paul McManus, president at McManus Kitchen and Bath in Tallahassee, Florida, recommends focusing on some simple organizers, such as vanity and medicine cabinet organizers. “Another easy way to add storage is to put a floating shelf or two over the toilet, especially in small bathrooms,” says McManus.

Another way to revamp a bathroom is to swap out existing hardware and fixtures—cabinet knobs and handles, towel bars, faucets, and the showerhead—with upgraded options. Modern finishes like brushed nickel or matte black are a quick way to create a more modern, polished look without having to invest in a larger project like replacing all the cabinetry, says Solis. Just be sure to keep the hardware consistent for a seamless look.

Replacing your showerhead is very easy and affordable; it boosts the look of the bathroom, saves water, and improves the experience of using your shower. McManus recommends choosing a dual-function showerhead, such as Delta’s In2ition line that features a detachable hand shower that can be used separately from or simultaneously with the showerhead.

The Keg towel warmer can be mounted to your wall or placed freestanding, and it holds two standard bath towels or a large robe. See our full review.

Upgrading the lighting in the space is a great value-minded way to improve a bathroom, says Craig Gritzen, founder and principal designer at Curated Style Collective in Salt Lake City, Utah.

“Consider upgrading light bulbs in your bathroom fixtures to switch-color white LED bulbs that toggle between daylight for grooming (6000K) and warm light for relaxing (3000k) to help promote a spa-like feel,” says Gritzen. If your budget allows, he also recommends upgrading lights from builder-grade to more design-forward fixtures that are damp-rated to make the space feel more luxe. It’s also effective to layer in soft lighting to create a warm, soothing atmosphere, which can be accomplished by installing dimmable light bulbs, sconces, and small table lamps.

Painting is still one of the best value upgrades that homeowners can tackle in a weekend, says Gritzen. He suggests choosing soft, warm whites; muted greens and blues; or other grounding earth tones for the walls to make a stark space feel more relaxing and spa-like. In addition, Solis recommends adding a fresh coat of paint to the vanity or cabinets. “Since bathrooms are smaller, this project is a fairly easy one with large visual impact,” notes Solis. If you’re not up for painting the entire bathroom, try simply cleaning up paint lines to help make the room feel noticeably fresher.

Another way to transform the vibe of a bathroom is to incorporate spalike elements that provide comfortable textures and refreshing fragrances. “New plush towels with matching tones, along with a bathmat and shower curtain, can have a large impact on the space,” notes Gritzen. Another way to increase the spa feel without breaking the bank is to install a few robe hooks to hang terrycloth robes.

Scent can also help a bathroom feel more Zen, says Gritzen. “Scent stimulates our olfactory system, which can be used strategically to promote relaxation,” explains Gritzen. He suggests setting up a diffuser with lavender, eucalyptus, or sandalwood essential oils to help promote relaxation.

Most carved pumpkins tend to get binned or left rotting on the curb once the candles burn out. Yet that leftover gourdish grin is packed with benefits for your soil, future plants, and wildlife

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first few days of November bring a familiar sorry sight, as pumpkins start piling up beside the trash cans, a few of them still grinning. Millions end up in landfills every year, where they break down without much air and give off greenhouse gases. That's a poor end for leftover Halloween pumpkins. In a garden, all that soft tissue could be breaking down into organic matter and feeding soil life – and that’s just the start.

If you took the time to grow pumpkins for Halloween, you know how much space, moisture, and fertilizer a single vine demands. All summer long, its leaves absorbed sunlight and pumped nutrients directly into its swollen fruit. Letting those nutrients leave your yard in a trash bag deprives your yard of valuable goodness that could be benefiting vegetable beds, feeding organisms and helping beneficial creatures. Even a carved pumpkin can have a second life as long as it hasn't been painted or coated.

Giving your post-Halloween gourds a productive second act is simple, fun, and satisfying. The only rule is that your fruit needs to be clean and free of contaminants. Any sections coated in craft paints, glitter, chemical sealants, or fake snow must be removed and tossed into the trash. Pull out any burnt candle stubs, melted wax, and battery-powered tea lights, and you are ready to put this fall bounty to work!

Turning post-holiday pumpkins into garden assets is a real no-brainer. Standard carving pumpkin varieties like Howden and Jack O' Lantern work especially well for the soil, because their flesh is tender and relatively easy to slice. Thicker, denser culinary and heirloom varieties (such as ribbed Cinderella, dusty-blue Jarrahdale, or warty Marina di Chioggia) offer firmer rinds that hold their shape for weeks, making them ideal where shape and rigidity are useful.

These fall projects work across every USDA hardiness zone, though local temperatures will determine how quickly your gourd decomposes. In cold northern regions (zones 3-5), freezing nights preserve carved pumpkins on porches longer, but freeze-thaw cycles eventually cause cell walls to collapse into watery slop, making early November the best time to act. In warm southern places (zones 8-10), elevated daytime temperatures accelerate mold and fruit flies, requiring immediate conversion into ground-based or wildlife-specific benefits.

Before tackling these projects, you need the right hand tools. A heavy-duty hori-hori knife is an excellent investment if you don’t have one, and can be used to simplify all kinds of cutting work. The Nisaku Hori-Hori from Amazon is great value and makes slicing through thick rinds a joy, and levers drainage holes through thick base walls without snapping. So find out exactly why your grinning pumpkin still has lots of goodness to give…

Tossing an intact pumpkin onto your compost heap can lead to disappointment. Its waxy rind acts like a raincoat, and depending on the variety and the weather, it could sit there for a long time with its skin intact. It needs breaking up first. Take a sharp spade or round-point shovel, and break the fruit down into fist-sized chunks to expose the flesh to soil bacteria and fungi.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Because the tissue is roughly 90% water, this green compost source needs plenty of dry browns mixed in. Balance every bucket of chopped pumpkin with two buckets of carbon-rich browns, such as shredded leaves, straw, or torn cardboard to keep the pile aerated. Turn the heap now and then. If space is tight, a single-chamber tumbler like the Vivosun Outdoor Dual Chamber Tumbling Composter, available from Amazon speeds up heat decomposition in a more compact way.

If your compost heap is overflowing, try direct trench composting in an empty veg bed. Dig a trench 18-24 inches (45-61cm) deep, in a bed reserved for heavy-feeding spring crops like sweet corn, squash, or tomatoes. Fill the bottom with chopped chunks and stomp them down. Backfill with 12 inches (30cm) of clean soil. Don’t go shallower, or neighborhood raccoons may smell it and dig it back up. Loose, well-drained soil can break it down in 2-3 months, but if you have heavy clay soil, you may still hit chunks of pumpkin a year from now, so be patient.

A healthy, mature Halloween pumpkin contains hundreds of plump seeds loaded with goodness. If your pumpkin grew with vibrant color and a firm rind, these seeds are prime candidates for saving for next year. Strain the tangled seed mass in a colander and massage it under a stream of cold running tap water to strip away the pulp. Spread the cleaned seeds in a single layer over non-stick parchment paper, a fine metal screen, or a ceramic plate. Let them dry in a warm, well-ventilated room out of direct sunlight for 2-3 weeks.

To test for dryness, try bending one: if it flexes, it still retains moisture, but if it snaps in half, your seeds are ready to store. Slide your dried seeds into breathable kraft paper seed envelopes. Pour them into paper seed envelopes, like the Seed Packet Kraft Envelopes, available from Walmart in packs of 100. Write the variety and date on the front, and store in a cool, dark drawer. Word to the wise, though: modern carving pumpkins are typically hybrids that won’t go true to type. Also, bees can cross-pollinate squash varieties across neighborhood zucchinis, so next spring’s seedlings may produce some wacky, unpredictable gourds.

Songbirds burn through vital fat stores as November temperatures drop, and a firm pumpkin makes a wonderful natural feeding bowl (although it’s best to stick to uncarved porch pumpkins for this project). Cut your pumpkin in half across the middle, or slice the top third off. Using a sturdy spoon or hori-hori to scrape out the inner pulp and seeds, until the interior walls are clean. Poke 3-4 half-inch (1.25cm) drainage holes through the base using a large screwdriver.

Punch 3 evenly spaced holes along the thick top rim, thread some sturdy jute twine through, and hang the bowl from a sturdy tree limb or pergola beam. Alternatively, set the flat shell on a low wall, tree stump, or deck railing. Fill with black-oil sunflower seeds or a good seed blend, such as Pennington Wild Bird Food from The Home Depot. You can also use some of your rinsed and dried pumpkin seeds as extra treats. These nutritious kitchen scraps make a nourishing treat for cardinals, blue jays and titmice. Just inspect every few days: when the inner walls turn squishy or develop fuzz, take the feeder down and consign it to the compost heap.

If you have a solid (again, uncarved) ornamental pumpkin on your porch, you can turn it into a temporary planter. Carve a generous opening around the stem and scoop out the pulp and seeds. Using a long screwdriver, puncture 4-5 generous drainage holes through the bottom crust. If you need a good screwdriver, Black Canyon’s Phillips Extended Length Screwdriver with Soft Grip Ergonomic Handle from Walmart is an efficient way to punch through thick rinds. Elevate the pumpkin on some stone or a trivet for drainage, as sitting water will rot the base rapidly.

Fill the lower half of the pumpkin with light, free-draining potting soil, then tuck in your choice of cold-tolerant fall ornamentals. Some great options include dwarf flowering kales, ruffled ornamental cabbages, winter violas, pansies, and trailing English ivy. These cold-hardy choices will look fresh and colorful for 2-4 weeks. With wet soil sitting inside it, the pumpkin starts softening from the inside out, and a few freeze-thaw nights will hurry it along. When yours starts to sag, move the plants to a bed or regular pot, and compost the gourd.

Slugs and garden snails are a persistent menace in fall, but at night they seek shelter in dark, damp, sheltered crevices to conserve moisture. A curved chunk of pumpkin rind provides a perfect natural decoy. Take sections of rind, including leftover pieces from carving or scraps that have softened too much for bird feeders. Place them skin-side up on the soil, beside vulnerable vegetable rows, hosta crowns, or mulched borders. The sweet scent of decaying squash flesh will attract slugs from several feet away, luring them under the hollowed domes.

Early the following morning, flip the rinds over. You should find dozens of slugs, snails, and earwigs clinging to the flesh. Scrape them off into a bucket of warm soapy water, or feed them to backyard chickens. Reset the traps for several nights in a row. Every slug removed now is one fewer laying eggs. Once the rind collapses, compost it. Dust a little Harris Food Grade Diatomaceous Earth Powder, available from Amazon, around your traps to stop slugs escaping back into your beds.

This last one is a lovely eco-friendly bonus for anyone keen to support overwintering beneficial insects in their yard. As fall frosts intensify, beneficial predatory insects and pollinators seek sheltered crevices. Ground beetles, centipedes, roving rove beetles, lacewings, lady bugs, and solitary native bees are valuable allies in the organic garden, consuming thousands of aphids, slug eggs, and weed seeds. You can turn a hollowed pumpkin shell into a cozy winter sanctuary. Take an uncarved or cleanly carved pumpkin. Slice a wide entryway near the base (or prop the shell upside-down on a couple of flat stones to leave an open gap underneath).

Stuff the cavity with natural textural materials that create micro-tunnels and air pockets. Use bundles of dry hollow plant stems, bamboo canes, small pine cones, crumpled dry leaves, and coarse straw. You can buy Bell Nursery Mini Straw Bales from The Home Depot which can also be used as mulch for strawberries and other overwintering plants. Tuck your bug hotel beneath a thick hedge, under a quiet shrub border, or along a perennial bed out of wind and rain. The shell will slowly soften, insulating the center. By spring, it will return harmlessly to the soil, leaving your beneficial guardians safely in the mulch bed, ready to go to work.

Before you drag your hollowed Halloween pumpkins down to the street corner, hopefully these ideas show you that they could be working hard for your yard. These seasonal gourds are far more than short-lived porch decorations. By turning into a rich soil ingredient, feeding wild birds, constructing cozy shelters for beneficial beetles and stocking up on seeds to plant next year’s pumpkins, you keep valuable resources out of landfills and grab a head start on next year's growth. Once winter sets in, those leftover gourds may already be enriching your soil: a true win-win!

After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.
