#7948. A Libertarian Perspective on the 2026 Election

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Why we should vote "Democrat by Default" for federal offices - with a few rare exceptions. I build on a post by political philosopher Dan Shapiro.

I was going to write a post about why, in this election, the right thing for libertarians to do is vote for Democrats for all federal offices, unless either 1) the Dem candidate is DSA, or 2) the GOP candidate is one of those very rare Republicans who oppose all or most of Trump's awful policies. But libertarian political philosopher Dan Shapiro beat me to it, in an excellent post at the Bleeding Heart Libertarian substack. I agree with the vast bulk of what he says. But I have a few additions and caveats that I will append after quoting a few key passages from Dan's post. Before getting into detail, I will note that I generally believe in voting for the lesser evil among those candidates with a realistic chance to win. Thus, unlike Dan, I don't usually vote for third party candidates, even in more normal times. If you're opposed to "lesser evil" voting on principle, we have a disagreement that goes  far beyond the present election. But I would urge you to check out my defense of that practice, where I explain why you should even vote for the evil Queen Cersei over the even more evil Sauron, if those are the only available choices.

I don't expect this post or Dan's will change the outcome of the election. They almost certainly won't. But they might still be helpful in thinking through big issues we face in the current political moment.

Most of my voting life I voted for the Libertarian Party when they advocated classical liberal/libertarian policies. Now those who care about and prioritize liberty and a free society—however they label themselves—should vote Democratic unless the candidate is a Democratic Socialist….

There's been so much criminality and misdeeds in the Trump administration that it's exhausting to cover it all, but keeping "the land of the free and the home of the brave" means remembering the essentials. I provide links when the points I make are not common knowledge and/or might be controversial.

January 6: Trump is the only presidential candidate in the US who refused to concede that he lost. He told a crowd to "fight like hell," and the mob then stormed the Capitol to try to overturn the results. The House impeached him for "incitement of insurrection," and 57 senators, including seven Republicans, voted to convict—short of the two-thirds required. After his campaign of lies and deception and pressuring election officials to falsify the results failed to overturn the election, he later pardoned all the perpetrators of the violence.

ICE: masked secret police who kidnap people and send them to hellholes in El Salvador, where they were subject to constant beatings, sexual abuse, and torture; to the Central African Republic, in the midst of a brutal civil war with severe human rights abuses; to Florida's "Alligator Alcatraz," where large numbers of detainees were held in cages the size of phone booths; and to Fort Bliss, Texas, where guards grabbed detainees' testicles while beating them. There've been zero consequences for this; indeed, Trump says they are "immune."

Not only were the deportations done without any notification to families or lawyers, but ICE has disappeared from databases those they seized so lawyers and families can't find them.

ICE and CBP have rammed people in their cars, dragged the occupants out, and rammed into houses without warrants. They have murdered, wounded, and assaulted protestors and ICE monitors—Alex Pretti and Renee Good, during the ICE occupation of Minneapolis, being the most publicized—but there have been many others.

There is now "expedited removal" for anyone undocumented, which means no hearing before a judge. (And this is even though immigration judges are—wrongly—a part of, and not independent of, the executive branch.) Indeed, Trump fired any immigration judge who disagreed with him or whom he perceived as not being deportation-friendly enough, and replaced the Board of Immigration Appeals, which has denied appeals for almost all deportation orders.

The administration removed TPS (temporary protected status) for immigrants fleeing violence and is deporting them to the very countries the State Department has declared unsafe—e.g., Haiti.

ICE apprehended immigrant parents after they dropped their kids off at school (see here, here, and here), as well as apprehending children and toddlers and using them as bait (the Liam Conejo Ramos incident)….

Trump sent Marines to LA, and National Guard troops to Chicago and DC. This violates a basic norm since the Founding and violates Posse Comitatus, a statute banning the military from policing.

Trump and FCC chairman Carr threatened talk shows and networks for dissenting political opinions.

As mentioned, ICE murdered, assaulted, and wounded protestors and ICE monitors.

The administration targeted people for their political views and for writing op-eds. Rochester resident David Streever sent a critical email to the director of ICE, and five months later, federal officers tracked his movements and staked out his New York City hotel as he returned from an overseas trip….

There is much more, including explanations of why the Democrats (with the notable exception of DSA types) are far less bad than this, despite their considerable flaws. I myself have written about the evils of the DSA here, explaining why they are comparable to MAGA nationalist Republicans.  In addition to the harm individual DSA members might cause if elected to office, it is important to reduce their numbers as much as possible, so as to minimize the chances that socialists could take over the Democratic Party, as MAGA nationalists have done with the GOP.

I have a few additions to Dan's arguments.

First, it is essential to consider the enormous scale of Trump's harmful and unjust immigration and trade policies. When it comes to setting issue priorities, scale matters a great deal. Even under normal administrations, immigration restrictions threaten the economic and civil liberties of American citizens (to say nothing of those of immigrants themselves) more than any other federal policy. Trump's vast expansion of exclusion and mass deportation has made things a lot worse. The liberty and well-being of millions of people are at stake.

Trump's trade policies seek to impose the highest tariff levels since those that gravely exacerbated the Great Depression, and also are a grave menace to the rule of law. Here too, we're talking about massive effects on the liberty and welfare of millions. Judicial review can and has helped curb these abuses (more on the tariff front than immigration). But there is much Congress can do to help, including curbing funding to ICE and other agencies complicit in wrongdoing. Congressional Democrats also plan to cut back executive tariff authority. That may not succeed while Trump remains in office, but can help set the stage for later progress.

Dan raises the issue of whether non-DSA Democrats might be worse than the Trump-era GOP on economic liberty issues. This becomes an easy issue if you recognize that immigration restrictions and tariffs are also violations of economic liberty. Due to their massive scale, Trump's actions in this area easily outweigh the very real economic policy flaws of non-DSA Dems. And then we have such things as his acquisition of federal government stakes in numerous private firms, something that even the most left-wing recent Democratic presidents didn't attempt. It's a dramatic example of how MAGA nationalists have dangerous economic policies similar to those of socialists.

It is also important to remember that a Democratic Senate could block Trump's horrible executive and judicial nominees. I don't want to see any more Pete Hegseths and RFK, Jrs. In Trump's first term, he had some good judicial nominees. In the second, he has mostly  bad ones (Emil Bove is a particularly egregious example). From a libertarian perspective, I'd rather have a standard liberal nominee fill the next Supreme Court vacancy (despite all the flaws such jurists have) than the type of right-winger Trump II is all too likely to nominate. Such a person would probably be selected for his willingness to turn a blind eye to executive abuses of power, trample civil liberties, and bulldoze constitutional obstacles to MAGA nationalist policies, such as federalism and separation of powers. There may well not be any Supreme Court vacancies, of course. But lower court nominations will arise, and they matter too.

Finally, I'm more hawkish than the average libertarian, and I think it's important to counter Trump's policies of undermining the Western alliance, and coddling mass-murdering dictators like Vladimir Putin and (to a lesser extent) Xi Jinping. We should care about defending liberty worldwide, not just in one country, especially since the two are interconnected. The Democrats (except for a few far-leftists) oppose this awfulness and could use control of Congress to help curb it.

In these and other areas, a Democratic-controlled Congress could not fully stop Trump's abuses. The executive has accumulated too much power for that, often in constitutionally dubious ways. But congressional control of nominations and purse strings can do much to constrain the executive at the margin. And electoral repudiation of Trump's abuses can reduce the risk that future presidents will imitate them.

I do have a few caveats to attach to Dan's otherwise compelling points:

First, Dan doesn't differentiate between elections for federal offices and those for state and local ones. I do. Beating the GOP in federal races is vital for countering Trump's awful agenda. At the state and local level, other issues are dominant, and Republicans are often better than Dems on the crucial issues of housing, state-level taxation, and state and local economic regulation. Which party is better on these and other state and local issues will vary from state to state. For example, red state Republicans are much better on the crucial issue of housing deregulation than blue state ones (who often back exclusionary zoning against Democratic reform efforts). Thus, it might make sense to vote for Republican candidates in some state and local races, but not others, depending on the issues involved.

Second, when it comes to the DSA problem, there can be difficult questions about what to do with Dem candidates who are not actual DSA members, but seem closely adjacent to them. Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is a notable example. He says he's not a socialist, but also is closely aligned with socialists like Bernie Sanders, and "influencer" Hasan Piker, the guy who - among other things - praises communist mass murderers like Mao Zedong.

In this post, I'm not going to try to adjudicate each individual candidate and race. I will merely say that if you're trying to figure out whether a non-DSA member is actually a socialist, two noteworthy indicators are 1) whether he or she supports government control of all or most of the economy and 2) whether they praise socialist despots abroad, such as Mao, Fidel Castro, and others. If the answers to one or both questions are "yes," that's a strong indication they might be socialists, and therefore not worth voting for, except perhaps against the very worst Republicans.

There is a similar calculation in identifying the few Republicans who have opposed Trump's worst policies. Here, key indicators are whether they have opposed his tariffs, his mass deportations, his kowtowing to Vladimir Putin, and his attacks on civil liberties. Sadly, Republican candidates with consistent strong records on all or most of these issues, are few and far between, though Republican criticism of the tariffs and policies towards Russia have picked up in recent weeks.

Finally, as Dan would agree, voting for Democratic candidates does not imply supporting everything the Democratic Party does, or abstaining from criticizing Democrats on the many occasions when they do bad things.

Elsewhere, I have argued that libertarians, in the current political moment, should seek an alliance with "abundance liberals." But alliance is not the same thing as total agreement. And the Democratic Party obviously includes various factions who are much worse than the abundance types. We should keep that in mind, even as we recognize that right now the Republicans are much worse.

#7947. Frost Coming Your Way? What to Do With Veggies in the Garden

Updated Oct 28, 2026 4:20 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

While some people welcome the cooling that accompanies autumn, gardeners know they have work to do before the coming frost kills off the literal fruits (and veggies) of their labor.

First, find out the typical frost dates for your USDA hardiness zone and learn what temperatures cause frost damage. Then, watch local weather forecasts. Understand the difference between frost and light freeze, and which plants are more susceptible to frost damage.

Start with healthy plants and the right soil. Next, you’ll need to know which plants are tender and which can withstand a light frost and which delicious homegrown fruits and vegetables you’ll need to harvest before it’s too late.

Tender plants are easily damaged by frost or cold weather, requiring protection to survive. Common tender fruits and vegetables include watermelon, squash, pumpkin, cantaloupe and muskmelon, eggplant, cucumber, okra, pepper, beans, tomatoes, and most herbs.

Frost-tolerant plants can withstand brief periods of cold or frost, but beyond very limited periods, would require protection. Examples of frost-tolerant plants include lettuce, cauliflower, endive, peas, carrots, Chinese cabbage, celery, chard, and chicory.

Hardy plants generally have higher levels of sugar in their leaves, which enables them to tolerate lower temperatures. Cool-season crops that can survive a frost or even an early freeze include asparagus, cabbage, kale, spinach, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, collards, potatoes, and onions.

Many crops can be saved from an early frost. Even cool-season crops like lettuce and other leafy greens, carrots, and radishes can benefit from overnight covering to protect the plants from frost and extend the growing season. You can use old sheets or drop cloths (using supports to keep the cover from touching the plants), burlap, row covers made of non-woven polyester, or cloches.

Whichever type of plant cover you choose, make sure it is breathable. Do not use plastic. Ensure air circulation and be sure to remove the covers during the heat of the day, and put them back on in the early evening.If you have a greenhouse, move as many plants as you can inside.

Bio Green’s heater has a digital thermostat, sturdy stainless steel build, and is intended for spaces up to 130 square feet. Read the review.

Adding a 2- to 4-inch layer of mulch, particularly in the afternoon while the soil is warm, can help protect roots from overnight dips in temperature. Material choices to minimize frost damage include wood chips, bark, pine needles, straw, and even shredded leaves (including if they’re moldy). Dark mulch absorbs more of the sun’s warmth, which it releases into the soil around the plants at night.

Mulching the garden also preserves much-needed moisture. In addition, a layer of mulch will prevent perennials from putting out new growth at the end of the season, allowing them to go dormant for the winter.

Moist soil actually holds up to four times more heat than dry soil, and conducts that heat to the soil surface faster, creating a microclimate in which the air above it is 5 degrees warmer. In addition to providing an insulating effect, water helps plants withstand temperature changes better.

For best results, water late in the day because the water vapor creates a microclimate that will help plants stay warm and resist freezing.

When all else fails, harvest what you can. Beans, peas, corn, melons, cucumbers, eggplant, and most greens should be harvested early, since they don’t handle frost well. Be sure to pick tender herbs such as basil and oregano.

Tomatoes and peppers can ripen indoors after harvest. In fact, many fruits, including apples, peaches, pears, grapes, cantaloupe, and persimmon, ripen after picking. Store pumpkins and squash in a dry location for later use.

It can be tough to eat all of the last harvest right away, but there are plenty of ways to preserve your bounty: dry herbs, and can, dry, or freeze fruits and vegetables.

Many fruits can ripen indoors more quickly if they’re kept in a paper bag that is loosely closed at the top. Storing them this way traps ethylene gas that helps ripen fruit. Because rice also traps ethylene gas, fruits can be placed in containers of rice, although this is not recommended for tender fruits such as peaches that can suffer bruising. Taking these steps can typically help fruit ripen within a few days.

Plastic bags are not advised for ripening fruit because they don’t allow for ventilation.

Not all produce has to be harvested at the first sign of frost. Many root vegetables, like beets, carrots, onions, turnips, parsnips, and potatoes can easily survive a light frost. So can kale, artichokes, broccoli, cabbage, radishes, leeks, spinach, Brussels sprouts, and chard. In fact, cold temperatures improve the flavor of crops such as carrots and kale.

Several of these can even survive a hard frost, including broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage, collards, kale, kohlrabi, mustard, onions, parsley, peas, radishes, spinach, turnips, leeks, and sorrel.

If frost gets your fruits and vegetables, they may not be edible. Tender plants like peppers, tomatoes, and many fruits may be mushy. Lettuces and other greens often turn dark and limp. Beans, eggplant, and potatoes are also susceptible to frost, and may exhibit crystalized moisture in their cells. Even carrots can become rubbery or limp after a hard frost.

If the produce is past its prime, dispose of it in your compost pile or bin, where it can benefit next year’s garden.

All You Need to Care for Your Lawn & Garden

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

#7946. 5 Easy Fall Wins to Help Your Backyard Birds Survive Winter – How to Beat the Big Chill and Ensure More Visits

Huddled in hedgerows and shedding trees this fall, your backyard birdies need your help. Here are the simple things you can do now to keep them healthy and happy through winter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall can be deceptive: for a while, the lingering sunlight might be warm, and there might still be pops of color as late-season annuals stand in defiance. But all it takes is one big cold snap or a nibble of frost for the whole yard to change, literally overnight. The transition from late fall color to the reality of several months of winter can be a shock – and not just for us. As we huddle over morning hot drinks and contemplate the gaps in the yard, imagine how it feels for our feathered chums.

From plump northern cardinals to energetic black-capped chickadees, these shifting conditions present a challenge for bird feeding, shelter, and survival. Tree cover is starting to bleed away as fall leaves spiral to the ground, exposing branches to biting winds, cold rain, and sharp frosts. The juicy bugs of July are history, dogwood berries are being stripped, and crisping soils mean foraging birds have to work twice as hard for every meal. For birdies that only weigh a couple of nickels, getting through the night means burning nearly an entire day’s energy just to stay warm.

So for our pint-sized backyard companions, the big chill isn’t just an inconvenience; it’s a fearsome calorie crunch. This narrow window in late fall is your best opportunity to step in with kind, targeted care. These little backyard wins won’t punish your wallet and they don’t demand much time. Just a little thoughtful prep today will keep your feathered neighbors safe, spunky, and singing outside your window all winter.

Preparing your backyard for happy wintering birds is all about timing. Whatever you do, don’t be tempted to put these little fall tasks off too long. I get it: in the whirl of leaf raking, perennial cutting, and hose winterizing, it’s easy to get distracted. But waiting until the first blizzard strikes and the ground freezes is a classic birdcare blunder, and one that tends to result in a yard devoid of birdsong.

Early winter is when resident birds establish foraging routes. By taking action now with these simple steps, you set up your yard as the place to stop mid-route – before the mercury plunges. Your USDA hardiness zone and regional climate have a part to play. In colder northern areas (zones 3-5), the risk of sudden hard freezes requires an earlier focus on high-density fats and ice-free water sources. Warmer zones 7-10 may host nomadic cedar waxwings and lingering eastern bluebirds as well as year-round residents. Yet they tend to share the same priorities: fast fuel, reliable drinks, and a cozy place to ride out a gale.

Before diving into these quick fall tasks, survey your yard. Observe how morning light strikes your patio, identify sheltered spots safe from north winds, and check that feeding and water stations are 10 feet (3m) from protective shrubs and safe staging or waiting branches for timid finches to peek out. Speaking of peeking, if you can’t afford a smart feeder, keep some compact binoculars or a monocular scope on hand to monitor visiting species and track which treats disappear first. The Pankoo 16x52 High Powered Monocular Telescope, available from Amazon, is a great way to enjoy shy songbirds on a budget.

Helping your birds thrive during winter starts now. These timely acts of care require minimal effort, and the payoff for getting your yard dialed in for the season is huge. By setting up your stations for winter, you’ll be rewarded with fluttery visitors even when the snow starts to fall. Here’s how easy it is to create a sanctuary for birds to fly in the face of the big chill…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As late fall chills settle in, backyard birds undergo a dietary pivot. During summer, they could thrive on lean insects and grains. But once night temperatures flirt with freezing, survival tilts towards fats. Burning fuel just to stay warm until breakfast is serious business. Now’s the time for you to swap out cheap summer filler seeds like red milo for lipid-rich options that deliver maximum energy per beakful.

This is the time to load your feeders with black-oil sunflower seeds. Their thin, papery shells are easily cracked by finches and chickadees, and their plump hearts are packed with plant oils. For ground-foraging juncos and sparrows, sprinkle hulled sunflower chips on low platforms so they don’t have to waste energy on dehulling. And hang some rendered suet cakes laced with berries or raw peanuts to nourish blue jays, red-bellied woodpeckers, downy woodpeckers, and nuthatches. C&S Peanut Suet Treat Cakes, available from Amazon, come in great-value packs.

Toss a handful of crunchy, dried mealworms onto a shallow tray to entice visiting eastern bluebirds and hermit thrushes to the party. Just make sure your feeder is able to support these extra nibbles, as well as allowing fall rains to drain freely. An open platform feeder, like the Kingsyard Hanging Platform Bird Feeder Tray from Amazon, can house a healthy fall feast in comfort while reducing the risk of mold.

Some of the simplest (and yet oddly, easily overlooked) fall birdcare measures involve your bird bath. Yes, topping up the seed hoppers and platform feeders is critical, but what’s worse is when the trusty bath is just left to freeze over. For birds, crunching on cold snow isn’t a fun winter pastime but an energy disaster. It drains their internal body heat precisely when they need every drop of warmth to survive.

It’s frustrating, because this is such an easy problem to avoid. At this time of year a heated bird bath, such as the Allied Precision Heated Bird Bath with Mounted Bracket, from Amazon, can pay for itself in terms of bird visits. Alternatively, you can keep water in motion (and so reduce freezing) by adding a rubber duck or ping pong ball to your bird bath. Ensure that the water depth in the bird bath remains shallow, never exceeding a couple of inches (5cm), so that small visitors like American goldfinches and purple finches can drink safely.

Drop in a flat, textured stone so little feet have a non-slip surface. Finally, keep water supplies fresher for longer by adding a copper disc to your bird bath. The Mellbree Bird Bath Copper Cleaning Disc from Amazon is a brilliant way to prevent algae build-up between cleans. Easy!

Sitting on a bare branch in a sharp November breeze is an everyday winter reality for your garden birds, but it is one you can help them with. Backyards are losing their natural windbreaks as deciduous trees drop their leaves, exposing birdies to the elements and also nocturnal prowlers. But you can bolster the availability of natural cover and create layered roosting pockets before deep winter sets in.

Late fall is an ideal time for planting certain key containerized native shrubs, such as Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry, available from Nature Hills, which establishes quickly in late fall, providing dense roosting cover and juicy berries for over 40 bird species. American beautyberry is another excellent bird-friendly native that you can also plant now, as long as you can tuck them in a few weeks before the ground freezes. You can pick up containers of Green Promise Farms’ American Beautyberry Live Plants from Amazon which will establish relatively fast. Remember to mulch with a 3-inch (8cm) ring of shredded bark.

Leaving dense conifers and arborvitae unclipped provides dense inner chambers where northern cardinals, dark-eyed juncos, and mourning doves can huddle. It’s also helpful to stack any thick trimmings you might have accumulated from fall pruning in a quiet border. A loose brush pile is perfect for winter wrens and ground-dwelling sparrows. Finally, you can convert unused wooden nest boxes into roosting cabins by sealing ventilation holes, flipping the front panel so the entrance hole sits at the bottom to trap rising heat, and layering the base with pine shavings.

At this time of year, it only takes a couple of heavy showers or sharp gusts to knock our bird-feeding routines into disarray. Even with the best intentions, we might put off bird feeder or bird bath cleaning, promising we’ll do it at the weekend, only to wind up catching up on box sets in our pyjamas (no judgments). But leaving a greasy ring of wet kernels or hulls stuck to the bottom of a feeder is a recipe for disaster, creating a breeding ground for killers such as Salmonellosis and Aspergillosis. Left unchecked, these can spread through the feathered community in a matter of days.

Establishing a rigorous weekly cleaning rhythm is your best line of disease defense. This can be as simple as a quick Sunday scrub routine (these can be surprisingly therapeutic!). It helps to have feeders that are easy to dismantle and clean in the first place. A good bird feeder option for weekly cleaning is the Woodlink Seed Tube Bird Feeder from Home Depot, with removable base ports that detach in seconds.

Once you have disassembled your seed tubes, hopper troughs, and platform trays, discard damp or caked seed remnants. Scrub tight nooks with an extra-long bottle brush, like the Songbird Essentials Extra Long Bottle Brush, available from Amazon. Then soak the parts for 10-15 minutes. Using a ratio of nine parts to one, dip in warm water laced with distilled white vinegar. Rinse thoroughly and ensure every component is dry before refilling. Sweep away soggy fallen hulls while you’re at it, to help out ground-foragers like juncos and mourning doves.

In the fall yard, pristine neatness can often be the enemy of wildlife survival. Many of the forager’s final treasures of the season may be tucked beneath curling leaf fall or wedged in that forlorn dangling seed head. Stripping away key perennial skeletons and scooping up fallen foliage deprive backyard birds of vital natural gifts. Such backyard litter costs you nothing to leave, and they keep your birds stocked up in other sleeping nibbles, such as dormant spiders and protein-packed pupae.

So leave perennial seed heads standing, kick a mound of leaves under your hedges, and let nature do the catering. Place a low, wire-mesh ground tray nearby, filled with a sprinkling of sunflower chips and crunchy protein-rich mealworms such as Kaytee Dried Mealworms from Walmart to reward their hard work. If you need a good ground tray feeder, the Mizxxidea Mesh Ground Bird Feeder from Amazon has an ultra-fine mesh base allowing fall rains to drain through cleanly. Blending handy extra feeding stations alongside natural foraging options creates the ideal birdie hangout.

These quick fall tasks are a lovely way of supporting your local birdlife as temperatures plummet, transforming your yard into a safe, high-energy refuge. While some of these fall extras are inexpensive, it’s worth investing in a few key features to help stay one step ahead of biting winds and winter chills. These curated staples will help you protect and nurture your resident songbirds from fall through winter.

Made of solid wood with a steep-pitched roof, this charming shelter offers visitors essential insulation against freezing drafts and rain. The side door makes cleaning simple, creating an ideal roosting cabin for chickadees, titmice, and wrens looking to huddle away from the worst of the winter weather.

This pretty jewel-toned basin is made from durable embossed glass and the textured presentation is kinder on birdie feet. It looks like high-end art, but is durable and rock-steady, although it's more likely to be filled with songbirds than hummers. Very easy to keep clean, and a real talking point for friends.

Crafted with vibrant stained-glass mosaic tiling, this fly-through feeder is great for shielding birds against winds and protecting seeds from drizzle. This pretty feeder's tunnel design also provides 360-degree visibility for skittish finches, chickadees, and nuthatches.

This timely fall intervention is all about making subtle, thoughtful shifts in our birdcare. By swapping in dense, high-calorie foods, maintaining easy-access water, supporting roosting options, cleaning feeders weekly, and leaving some fallen leaves around, you provide vital comfort and protection for vulnerable birds just when they need it most. It’s worth it to watch a puffed-up cardinal chewing on a mealworm, or a towhee poking out of some crunchy leaf litter, knowing that you’re doing your bit to keep nature’s sweetest living colors fluttering in and out of your yard.

She’s taken part in a range of conservation and rewilding projects for the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) and the British Trust for Conservation Volunteers (BTCV) as a way of exploring her horticultural horizons. #7945. How to Wrap a Tree to Protect it From Winter Damage

Published Oct 28, 2026 4:53 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

It may sound like an odd practice, but wrapping a tree can be worthwhile. Once trees drop their leaves, they no longer benefit from their protective canopy, and hazards can damage young and thin-barked trees, along with some evergreen trees and shrubs. “Cold temperatures, drying winds, ice, and hungry wildlife can injure trees during winter,” says Fred Breglia, ISA, a certified arborist and author of the upcoming book titled Big Trees: A Tour of the World’s Biggest Trees.

And it’s not just the cold that makes trees susceptible to damage. Adding a tree wrap around the trunk can protect the bark from harsh winter sun when leaves no longer shade it. Ahead, learn why tree wrapping helps some trees flourish and survive colds—and how you can wrap trees for winter safely and effectively.

Young trees, like those that have been growing for up to two seasons, are especially susceptible to winter damage. Wrapping immature and thin-barked trees helps prevent trunk damage from sun and freeze-thaw cycles. Some evergreens also benefit from a full-tree wrap for winter or a screen to prevent browning foliage, and other young trees can be saved from animal munching or rubbing damage with a fence wrap.

Rapid temperature changes in winter combine with an empty canopy to expose trees to frost cracks or sunscald. Vertical frost cracks can make a tree more vulnerable to pests or diseases.  Sunscald is even more serious. “Sunlight warms frozen bark, then shade or nightfall causes it to refreeze and die,” says Breglia. Sunscald usually occurs on a trunk’s southwest side, where winter sun is most intense and the bark warms up the most. It can cause a jagged vertical wound along the tree trunk and dry, cracked, sunken, or dead bark.

Trees are more susceptible to sunscald include those less than 2 years old and species with thin bark, such as:

Another type of cold damage is winter browning, or desiccation injury, which “occurs when evergreen needles and rhododendron leaves lose moisture faster than frozen soil can replace it,” says Breglia. He adds that low temperatures, freeze-thaw cycles, sun, and wind can worsen winter damage on evergreens or semi-evergreens. “Browning often occurs on the south or southwest side of conifers, though wind exposure may also damage the north side,” Breglia says.

Trees and shrubs most susceptible to winter browning include broadleaf evergreens, needled evergreens, or those with scale-like leaves, such as:

Deer and other browsers can munch on buds of trees in winter when food is scarce, but they also can bite into tender bark. Even in early fall, bucks look for small tree trunks to rub against as new antlers form and cause itching. “Voles, mice, and rabbits can severely damage young trees and shrubs by eating their bark in winter,” adds Breglia.

As always, young trees are most vulnerable to severe damage, along with some trees that wildlife prefer.

If you have a young tree or a tree or shrub species vulnerable to winter damage, you generally need to learn how to use tree wrap so you can prepare it in fall before the first winter frost. The precise timing varies by region and the type of damage that can occur. For example, if deer visit your landscape, you might need to wrap young trunks by late summer or as soon as you see bucks growing antlers.

For potential vole and mice damage, wrap trunks before the first snowfall. Most young trees will benefit from wrap protection for at least two winter seasons. In all cases, be sure to remove tree wraps by spring and never leave them on all year.

The most common way to wrap a tree trunk for winter tree protection is with a poly or fabric tree wrap or plastic guard. A tree wrap should be breathable and a light color. Breglia says the material should “conform to the trunk but also allow airflow without trapping moisture.”

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

Using a small trowel or shovel, gently scrape away any debris or leaves against the trunk and dig about 1 inch below the soil surface all around the trunk. This helps to set your tree wrap taut against the trunk and just below ground level.

Start at the lowest point of trunk exposure and begin to wrap around the trunk, ensuring each pass overlaps by at least ⅓ of the wrap’s width so there is no exposed bark.

If you’re using a plastic guard, widen the opening and place it around the tree, ensuring it sits just below ground level.

Continue to wrap the trunk until you reach the area just below the tree’s lowest branch. When you’re finished wrapping, secure the wrap with heavy-duty tape or twine. Do not staple or puncture the tree.

If using a plastic guard, add another guard above the lower one, cutting it if necessary to end just below the branches. Secure it to the bottom guard per manufacturer directions or with heavy-duty tape.

Check the wrap from time to time to make sure it remains secure at the top and has not loosened or been damaged below.

When the cold weather is over, carefully remove the wrap from the tree.

Although you can loosely wrap an entire shrub or tree in burlap to prevent winter browning, it is best to build a barrier around the plant, typically with stakes. “Use a burlap windbreak placed a few inches from the foliage, or loosely wrap multistemmed evergreens to block drying winter winds without trapping moisture,” says Breglia. If you wrap a tree or shrub in the fabric to protect it from wind or moisture loss, leave a hole at the top to allow sun and air to get in.

If you want to prevent winter wind damage like browning, install a burlap or shade fabric screen around the tree. Here’s how:

As long as your tree wrap is secure and at least 1 inch below ground, it can protect the trunk from most small animal damage. If you only need to protect against animals and not sunscald or browning, consider this method suggested by Breglia:

When wrapping trees for winter, always remember to remove the tree wrap in spring. Each spring, check trees and shrubs for any damage as growth resumes, like discolored needles, split bark, or areas that appear to have been nibbled on or stripped by animals. Breglia also advises watering trees well in spring and summer (and after planting a tree) so they are healthy when entering the winter season.

When properly placed, tree wrap can protect many trees and shrubs from winter damage. The trunks of young and thin-barked trees are particularly vulnerable to frost cracks, sunscald, and animal damage, so covering the trunk can keep a tree from the type of damage that could eventually result in taking the tree down and replanting.

Tree trunks are best wrapped in light-colored breathable fabrics especially designed for tree wrapping or plastic tree guards that surround a trunk. Some gardeners use burlap, but it can result in damage and is best used as a light wrap or screen to protect trees from winter browning or animal damage. Breglia recommends against the use of wound paint or dressing for young trees; paint will not protect trees from animal damage.

Always wait to wrap a tree in fall as it goes dormant and before the first hard frost. If you miss the first frost, wrap the tree as soon as the trunk has dried out to prevent repeated injury. Never wrap or leave wrap on a tree in spring or summer growth phases. And the best time to wrap a tree is when it is young (first 1 to 3 years of growth).

Some trees or shrubs need only temporary winter protection from unusual frosts or storms. A burlap screen or windbreak also can protect trees in winter. Spreading a 2- to 3-inch layer of mulch around the tree, at least the width of its root ball or canopy, can protect tender roots from repeated winter freezing and thawing. Breglia says that anti-dessicant sprays can help prevent drying out of trees and shrubs. Fencing can keep browsing animals away from evergreens.  “Proper placement of winter injury-sensitive plants, such as rhododendrons, boxwood, yew, or arborvitae can reduce the chance of winter damage,” adds Breglia. Finally, healthy trees can best survive winter, so watering and other care steps in spring and summer help protect tender trees in winter.

All You Need to Care for Your Lawn & Garden

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

Dreo has a winner with the Dreo WH517S smart space heater. We liked being able to hang this space heater on the wall, where it was up and out of the way, rather than sitting on a wet bathroom floor. Installation was simple: Dreo included a mounting template that indicated the location for the screws, and best of all, the template came with a bubble level so that we could ensure the heater would be perfectly straight.

Setting up the app was a snap. All we had to do was plug the Dreo WH517S into the wall socket and turn it on. We already had the Dreo app on our smartphone, which immediately recognized the heater. If you don’t have the app, a QR code walks you through the steps.

This heater also comes with an ALCI plug option capable of shutting the heater off when it senses abnormal electric flow. It also has an IP24 rating, so it can take an occasional splash of water. In homes with small children, this heater can be mounted high on the wall for added safety.

What our tester says: “On winter mornings, I love being able to turn on the heater in the bathroom from my smartphone without having to get out of bed. Just 15 minutes and the bathroom is warm and comfortable for my shower.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

You don’t have to spend a lot to warm up a chilly bathroom. The Lasko 1500W bathroom space heater is compact, comes with an ALCI safety plug, and best of all, is affordable.

This Lasko heater doesn’t have many bells and whistles, but it’s a solid pick to heat a small- to medium-size bathroom. It measures just 8 inches tall by 6.25 inches wide and weighs just 3.35 pounds, making it small enough to sit on a bathroom shelf or countertop.

When we started researching modern bathroom heating options, we quickly discovered that there were hundreds of different models available. After carefully considering nearly 50 choices, we settled on eight top models, and then we chose four of those to test in our own bathrooms.

We also looked at how safe the various models were for use in standard bathrooms. Remodeling expert Benjamin Stenson, director of operations of Norsemen, a home remodeling contractor in Louisville, Kentucky, told us, “Safety features are paramount, so users must opt for heaters designed to withstand bathroom conditions.”

Hands-on testing consisted of assessing the quality of each heater’s build, trying out each of its features, and keeping records of how quickly each one heated a small bathroom during cold weather. We noted how hot the exterior of the heaters became after an hour of continuous use, and we awarded points based on a rubric—the better a bathroom heater performed on a test or assessment, the higher the points. After testing, we summed the points and used them to determine our best overall pick and assign relevant categories for the others.

While the appearance of a bathroom heater will always impact choice, there are a number of technical aspects to consider. The information below will help shoppers choose the most appropriate types of electric bathroom heaters for their needs.

The three general types of heaters for bathrooms include portable bathroom heaters, wall-mounted heaters, and ceiling-mounted heaters. Most (but not all) space heaters for bathroom use are electric. It’s harder to find non-electric heaters than electric heaters for bathroom use.

The term “portable” can refer to various bathroom heaters, including plug-ins, space heaters, and oil-filled radiators. These are usually among the most affordable bathroom heaters. Their distinguishing design feature is that they are not permanently fitted to the bathroom wall or ceiling, so they can be used in other rooms. Some are very light and easy to move. Space heaters often have carry handles. Although oil-filled radiators are heavier, they can still be moved if necessary. All of these might be good options for bathrooms not in regular use, such as in a guest accommodation.

The main advantage of wall-mounted bathroom heaters is that they don’t take up valuable floor space. They can also be very discreet. Wall-mounted exhaust fans are sometimes combined with heater elements, though these generally have more modest output.

Much like wall-mounted models, a ceiling-mounted bathroom heater can be both powerful and discreet. Its position also keeps it well away from small children and pets. Many are combined with an exhaust fan, which is a benefit but can complicate installation. Some ceiling models are infrared space heaters that use a large red bulb to radiate heat downward.

Physical size will have an impact on choice, especially in smaller bathrooms. Plug-ins and small bathroom heaters can be an effective option, though recessed wall units and ceiling models have no space penalty at all once installed.

Actual heat output can be difficult to assess on an electric heater. Most indoor room heaters are rated in watts. Opinions vary, but many experts quote 5 to 10 watts per square foot as optimal for comfortable warmth. However, manufacturer figures may contradict this rule of thumb and are perhaps a better guide. Models described as providing “supplemental” heat might also fall below this standard, but it does depend on bathroom size. Bathroom heaters that provide thermostats or two output settings offer greater control over personal comfort.

Water and electricity are a dangerous mix, with a risk of serious electrical shock. The descriptive materials for any heater intended for use in the bathroom should clearly state that it is for bathroom use, but we could not find any official guidelines. Ceiling heaters for bathrooms present little risk when installed correctly because there are no exposed heater elements or plugs.

Other units may be at risk of water splashes, so thought should be given to positioning. In addition, there is some risk at wall outlets. The usual solution is to fit either an ALCI or GFCI safety plug. Both will cut power in a fraction of a second and prevent harm. Many manufacturers provide these, but they can also be retrofitted.

Some use portable propane heaters in bathrooms and other interior rooms, but if you choose that option, make sure the heater is designed for inside use. Some will give off dangerous fumes.

There’s a lot of detailed information in the article above, and we hope it answers most questions that often crop up regarding choosing the best bathroom heater. While doing our research, we came across some queries of a more general nature, and we have addressed those here.

The best way to heat a small bathroom is often with either a portable heater, a fan-less wall panel, or a heated towel rack for the bathroom. These provide sufficient heat but are either very quiet or completely silent.

Bathroom heaters are absolutely worth it, as anyone who has had to bathe in a cold bathroom will attest. What’s more, many are very affordable as well as economical to run, so users can have a little luxury without a big bill.

Many different types of heaters are allowed in bathrooms, ranging from low-cost portable models to a variety of wall- and ceiling-mounted options. Our collection of top bathroom heaters listed above underlines the wide choice available.

Bathroom heaters are perfectly safe to use when installed and operated following the manufacturer’s recommendations. Sometimes it’s as simple as having an ALCI safety plug fitted. With others, the wiring is hidden and out of harm’s way.

It’s not a good idea if it’s a continuously running heater. However, if you have a permanently installed heater that runs on a thermostat, it’s probably okay. For trips to the restroom at night, consider a heated toilet seat and leave the space heater off.

Use 10 watts per square foot of floor space as a guide when sizing any kind of heater. For example, a 1500W bathroom heater will warm a 150-square-foot bathroom efficiently.

If it’s hardwired, probably. If it’s a high-capacity heater (1500W or up) that plugs into an outlet, it could overload the circuit if several other appliances are plugged in at the same time.

If you’re planting bulbs in your garden this fall, try this simple but super-effective hack to stop squirrels digging up tasty tulips and ruining the spring show.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Freshly planted spring-flowering bulbs provide an easy feast for hungry garden critters as temperatures drop, and are often eaten before they even get a chance to grow roots. Tulip bulbs are always the first to be sniffed out as they taste sweet and provide the perfect high-calorie meal for chipmunks as well as squirrels. Crocus bulbs, too, are carb-rich favorites on the garden menu in fall.

If you’ve experienced squirrels digging up tulip bulbs, you’ll know what determined diggers they are. Gardeners are just as dogged, however, and popular tricks to protect spring-flowering bulbs include laying steel mesh or chicken wire over the top, disguising the appealing scent of tulip and crocus bulbs by planting unappetising allium bulbs alongside, and using bulb baskets. But there’s a far easier, cheaper and more effective way to stop squirrels eating bulbs, and it helps the bulbs grow well, too.

What’s more, this robust solution protects bulbs from rodents and other underground burrowers like voles, who also love to seek out this nutrient-dense food source in fall.

When you're planting bulbs in fall, the magic ingredient to keep these energy balls safe from squirrels is poultry grit made from crushed oyster shells. The sharp, jagged edges of crushed oyster shells means it's painful for paws to dig through, so it provides an effective barrier that stops critters eating tulip bulbs and even tempting crocus.

What's more, as well as keeping bulbs safe from sharp teeth this natural material improves soil drainage, making bulbs less likely to rot through wet winter weather. Crushed oyster shells also break down very slowly to provide plants with a steady supply of calcium, which supports strong root and stem growth.

Not all chicken grit is created equal when it comes to protecting fall-planted bulbs, however. Make sure you buy chicken grit like Pacific Pearl Oyster Shell Calcium Supplement for Chickens, available from Walmart, that's made purely from oyster shells as many products are cut with cheaper materials like limestone. Choose crushed shells (sometimes sold as chick grit) over flaked shells as this is both sharper on paws and easier for plant roots and shoots to grow through.

When planting bulbs in pots, simply add an inch-thick layer of chicken grit to the soil surface to deter squirrels from digging, where it will also act as a mulch.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Opt for a double layer of poultry grit when planting bulbs in the ground. Add an inch-thick layer of crushed oyster shells to the bottom of the planting hole, and sit the bulbs right on top. This helps to protects bulbs from burrowing pests who typically attack from below, when a landslide of sharp oyster shells will send them scurrying away in search of more easily accessible food. If voles, field mice and pocket gophers are a particular problem in your garden, you can also pack a shallow layer of grit all around the bulb to fully encase it.

Fill the planting trench with soil as normal but add a second inch-thick layer of oyster shell grit an inch or two below the surface. When squirrels or other critters hit this sharp, gravelly layer, they’ll give up digging. This top layer can also help deter raccoons and skunks who don’t eat bulbs but are attracted to freshly-dug soil to look for insects and grubs.

Crushed oyster shells will naturally improve soil drainage and create beneficial pockets of air, loosening up heavy soil. The shells also release calcium as they break down, which plants need to build cell walls.

Adding a heap of oyster shells to your soil can affect its pH levels long-term but this hard material breaks down so slowly, that’s not a problem unless you have soil that’s already very alkaline. While some bulbs like camassia (wild hyacinths) prefer acidic soil, more palatable tulip and crocus bulbs both tolerate mildly alkaline soil just fine. Testing your soil with simple pH test strips like these from Amazon will instantly give you an answer if you suspect your soil is highly alkaline.

There are so many striking spring-flowering bulbs to plant in November, and using this clever trick will keep them safe from hungry animals in fall. Whether you view squirrels as garden pests or like to welcome wildlife into your garden, crushed oyster shells are a natural solution to prevent them digging up freshly planted bulbs in fall. Poultry grit is as economical as it is effective, too, so you get to enjoy those beautiful blooms come spring without spending a fortune.

Those splitting their own logs into more manageable sizes or kindling want a good axe, and few can match the quality or performance of the Estwing Fireside Friend. A 2⅜-inch hand-sharpened tempered-steel cutting edge ensures it slices through tough logs with minimal effort. A ballistic nylon sheath protects the edge when not in use. The handle is wrapped in a patented shock-reduction grip that absorbs up to 70 percent of the impact energy, dramatically reducing the chances of stress-related injuries.

Get the Estwing fireplace tool at Amazon.

When selecting the best fireplace tools, the challenge is finding the right blend of strength, durability, and style. What suits one person could be entirely inappropriate for another. In every case, manufacturing quality is the prime consideration, but caveats exist. Sometimes, high-value fireplace tools, while functional, may not have the strength of those manufactured by premium brands.

Nicole Cullum, interior designer and founder of the wallpaper and textile company Color Caravan based out of Taos, New Mexico, has helpful design advice when it comes to choosing fireplace tools: “Fireplace tools are most certainly an opportunity to blend function and design.” While they need to be long lasting, there is also the opportunity for “turning a basic tool into an artistic sculptural moment.”

Safety is also important. Fire Program Specialist Bruce D. Bouch, MPIO, of the U.S. Fire Administration says: “It is important to purchase quality tools that will not readily fail during use. Check the connections on the tools for stability and the quality of the stand if provided.” He also cautions that “ash collection should only be completed with a metal can with a tight-fitting lid designed for that purpose. Embers from a fire become insulated within the remaining ashes and can readily ignite combustible items.”

While every fireside tools set is designed to perform the same basic functions, a number of factors affect their suitability for a particular location, including decor style, size, material, number of tools included, and more. Below are details about key considerations shoppers often keep in mind while choosing the best fireplace tools.

While product photography can provide a detailed impression of the style of a particular fireplace tool set, it can be misleading in terms of size. For example, a set that looks heavy duty might actually be much shorter than depicted.

Always check the set’s physical dimensions. Tool length is not always provided, but knowing the overall height of the stand allows a reasonably accurate estimate. Width and depth of the set also can have an impact, depending on its intended location.

Fireplace tool sets usually include four pieces: a poker (or stoker), tongs, broom (or brush), and shovel (or pan), and the stand to complete what is typically called a five-piece set. Some sets omit the tongs.

Fireplace tools are usually made of brass, steel, stainless steel, or wrought iron.

Brass is decorative, but it has limited strength because brass sets were originally intended for coal fireplaces, not logs. Anyone installing a faux fireplace or gas fireplace might buy a brass set as decoration, but it’s not recommended for day-to-day use.

Wrought iron is more resistant to corrosion than brass and likely to be more durable, so it’s usually recommended for outdoor use. Wrought iron will rust eventually, and both plain steel and wrought-iron fireplace tools often have an additional coating for increased protection.

Stainless steel is highly resistant to rust but almost always more expensive. Considerable debate exists as to whether steel or wrought-iron tools are stronger. It depends on the steel composition and, with fireplace tools, that information usually isn’t available.

Consider how the shovel and broom are attached to their shafts as this also can impact durability. Shovels may be welded or riveted; the former is usually stronger. Brooms may have a replaceable head, but not always.

Traditional wrought-iron fireplace tools were naturally blackened or grayed during the forging process. Today, unless they’re handmade, the wrought-iron tools either will be painted or, more likely, have a tough powder-coated finish. The handles might be chromed or brass plated. While brass lacks strength on its own, as a coating, it is acceptable.

Style is very personal, and there are many designs to consider. Rope work is common, as are twists and scrolls. Other tools can be quite plain and minimalist. While decorative elements are always a key consideration, the functionality shouldn’t be overlooked. It’s particularly important that fireplace tools are easy to grip. If there’s an existing fireplace screen, consider tools that match that item.

Stability is also key. It’s almost inevitable that the fireplace tool stand will get bumped at some point. A flat base plate works well on a perfectly even floor but also check the material thickness. If it’s thin and lightweight, it might get knocked over easily. Those stands with four or five feet will probably balance better on surfaces that aren’t perfectly level.

When fireplace tools are purchased online, a modest amount of assembly may be required. The tool support stem may need to be attached to the base of the stand, for example. If a log basket is part of the set, it may need to be bolted together. Generally, a screwdriver and/or wrench is all that’s required.

The following is a quick guide to tool use:

After reading about the key features of the best fireplace tools and reviewing some of the best options on the market, you might still have some questions. Take a look at answers to some of the most commonly asked questions below to find the one you need.

If fireplace tools are left in the fire, it’s possible that they may get hot. However, generally, they are used briefly and then returned to the rack.

It can be. If you have a large open fire or an outdoor fire pit, short tools can bring your hands uncomfortably close to the flame. On the other hand, long heavy-duty tools can look out of place with a smaller fireplace.

A few are available, but the range is limited, and they frequently come close to the price of a whole new broom.

Many fireplace tools are designed to be used outdoors. A finish—like a powder coating—that protects them from corrosion or rust is a key feature. However, some are recommended for indoor use only, so always check the manufacturer’s recommendations.

Little leaves on an orchid's old flower spike may signal trouble – but a keiki doesn’t always mean the plant is struggling. Here's how to tell the difference.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It usually gets spotted by accident, halfway through watering. The flower spike that finished months ago has a few green leaves sticking out partway up, and maybe a stubby root or two hanging under them. That's an orchid keiki. For a minute, finding one feels like getting a second orchid for nothing.

Then the doubt sets in. Read up on what a keiki is, and you'll soon come across the idea that orchids are more likely to sprout them when they're stressed or failing. Anyone whose plant has also dropped a leaf or two lately will find that hard to shake.

Stress can play a part, though it's far from the only thing. Heat, fertilizer, and genetics all factor in, and plenty of keikis grow on plants with nothing wrong at all. A few minutes at the sink with the parent plant will tell you more than the keiki does itself.

The name is Hawaiian – keiki (KAY-kee) means baby. Look closely at a moth orchid (Phalaenopsis) spike, and you'll see small bumps along it, each wrapped in a papery sheath. Those are nodes, each holding a dormant bud, and once in a while one of those buds grows leaves. What grows is a miniature copy of the parent.

Keikis aren't an orchid disease or a parasite, and they can't spread to your other plants. They're simply one way orchids reproduce without seed. Where it grows matters more. A spike keiki sits up on the flower stem. A basal keiki comes up at the bottom, squeezed in next to the lower leaves, and on a moth orchid, that second kind can point to trouble at the crown.

A stem keiki growing on a Phalaenopsis orchid stem

Sometimes a keiki does show up because the parent is in trouble. Moth orchids grow from one point only, right in the middle of the leaves. Lose that tip to rot, or a break, and no new leaves can form up there. With energy in reserve, the plant may instead push out a basal keiki below the damaged tissue. Dendrobium canes that lose their roots, or their link to the rest of the plant through rot or injury, sometimes sprout keikis as well.

Plenty of keikis turn up on orchids with nothing wrong, though. On moth orchids, they come naturally from the middle and upper nodes of the spike, and certain species and hybrids are just more prone to it. Hormones are what flip a dormant bud into a keiki. Dab cytokinin, one of those growth hormones, on a node and it can pull a keiki out of a perfectly healthy plant. Crazy Keiki Cloning Paste, available on Amazon, is a well-rated product that contains cytokinin.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Long spells of heat as a spike finishes, heavy nitrogen feeding late in the season, and too little light or humidity have also been tied to keikis.

Some longtime growers take a keiki as a sign orchid care could use adjusting – a dim corner or heavy feeding is a good place to start. On a plant with firm, flat leaves and plump roots, a spike keiki usually isn't hiding anything. A basal keiki pushing up beside a soft, dark center is the one to worry about.

A basal orchid keiki growing on plant with some shriveled old roots

Start by checking for orchid leaf problems. Healthy moth orchid leaves are thick and firm, almost leathery. An occasional yellow bottom leaf is normal – the oldest leaves dry up as the plant ages. Several leaves yellowing at once is another matter, and so are newer leaves that have gone limp and wrinkled. Leaves that shrivel like that usually aren't getting enough water. And in fall, don't be fooled by a cold windowsill – nights below 60°F (16°C) can yellow lower leaves on their own.

Next, slide the pot off and check the orchid roots. Good ones feel firm and plump. They look green right after watering and silvery once they dry. Rotted ones are brown and mushy, and if you pinch one, the outer layer may slip off, leaving nothing but a thin string.

Now peer into the middle where new leaves come from. That's the crown. It should be firm and green. If it has gone soft, black, or wet-looking, crown rot has likely set in, often from water molds such as Pythium ultimum and Phytophthora cactorum, and rot that spreads through the crown can kill the whole plant.

One yellow leaf proves very little. Slow decline is different. If the leaves feel a little softer each time you check and nothing about the care has changed, look underground – usually at the roots, or at old bark mix that's broken down into soggy muck. Good news shows up in the same places. New leaves unfolding from the crown, or fresh green root tips near the base, mean the plant is still growing.

A basal orchid keiki has been left to grow into an established offshoot on this neglected plant

Did everything look fine? Then leave the plant alone, keiki and all. If the check turned something up, fix that and only that. Cut rotted roots back to firm tissue with something small and sharp, and wipe the blades with rubbing alcohol between plants. Fiskars' micro-tip pruning snips are narrow enough to get in between roots.

For repotting, use a specialist orchid potting mix, like Better-Gro Phalaenopsis mix, available at Home Depot, which is a fir bark blend. Use a clear slotted orchid pot, like these Holanhing pots, so you can keep an eye on the roots.

After that, water orchids sparingly until new roots reach the fresh bark, and water in the morning so the leaves dry before dark. Tip out any water that pools in the crown. Moth orchids do well in bright, indirect light, just not pressed up against cold glass or sitting above a heating vent.

The keiki itself can stay put. Without roots of its own, a spike keiki draws water and nutrients through the parent's flower stem, and snipping it off does nothing for rotting roots or a damaged crown. Many growers leave a moth orchid keiki alone until it carries a couple of leaves and roots about 1–1.5 inches (2.5–4 cm) long. Smaller ones often struggle on their own. Once it reaches that size, separating and potting the keiki is a quick way to propagate your orchid.

It depends on the damage. A moth orchid that still has some plump roots and a firm crown can come back once its care is fixed, though you may wait a while for the first new leaf. Rot through the crown is a much tougher case. So is a pot where you find almost nothing but mush. Even then, a plant with enough energy stored up can sometimes send up a new plantlet from its base.

This is where a keiki helps. It grew from the parent's own tissue, so it carries the same genetics and can keep that orchid going if the parent doesn't make it. Leave it attached while the parent holds up.

What if a declining plant has a green flower spike but no keiki? Try using keiki cloning paste, mentioned above, to coax one out, though results vary.

So it’s not time to write that orchid off, just yet, because of one odd growth. Check the plant it's growing from. If the leaves are firm and the roots and crown look good, the keiki is no warning at all, just a free second orchid hitching a ride on the first. With a little TLC, you can get that orchid blooming beautifully in no time.

#7937. 5 Spots for a Water Leak You Might Totally Miss—But Can Cost You

Published Oct 29, 2026 4:05 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Plumbing lines run throughout the home and the yard, bringing in fresh water for you to bathe, wash, water, and drink. However, when there is an issue with one of these plumbing lines or the attached appliances and fixtures, what seems like a small leak can quickly become a major problem as the growing accumulation of water causes water damage, encourages mold growth, and slowly ruins existing plumbing connections.

According to the EPA, the average household’s leaks can account for more than 9,300 gallons of wasted water per year, while some homes have leaks that waste 50 gallons or more per day. As a plumber and restoration expert, I have seen many issues that were easy enough to fix turn into major restoration projects simply because they were unseen or neglected for so long.

Even a single leak can destroy insulation, ruin drywall, and cause mold to spread behind your walls. Before your plumbing becomes a problem, use this guide to discover five water leak sources you might miss so that they don’t cost you in the long run.

Since this is a battery-powered unit, you don’t have to worry about missing a leak just because the power is out. Learn more in our buyer’s guide.

Water-carrying appliance hoses, like those on refrigerators, dishwashers, and washing machines, are notorious for causing catastrophic, hidden water damage. Since these appliances are often pushed tight against walls or tucked inside cabinetry, a slow leak can be difficult to find as it quietly rots the subfloor for months before a puddle ever creeps out into the open room.

The wax ring or plastic flange connecting the toilet base to the waste pipe can degrade over years. Instead of leaking onto the bathroom floor, the water can seep straight down through the subfloor, rotting the ceiling framing of the room directly underneath, which is why you need to be aware of any potential signs of a water leak, especially in the bathroom.

Water leaks caused by frozen pipes hidden behind walls or under concrete slabs can go unnoticed for a long time, causing extensive water damage in the walls if you aren’t careful. Water lines running beneath a concrete slab foundation can corrode or shift, causing a slow leak. These are highly hidden and usually only identified by a warm spot on the floor, a spike in the water bill, or eventual foundation cracking.

Underground irrigation lines are one of the most common culprits behind massive, hidden water loss. Because irrigation systems are buried across a wide outdoor area, an underground leak can dump thousands of gallons directly into the soil without ever creating a surface puddle.

Like roof leaks, outdoor spigots can lead to unexpected damage over a long period of time. These spigots should be turned off during the winter to prevent them from bursting internally during winter freezes. However, they may also develop leaks during the warmer months of the year, and the leak can remain completely hidden inside the wall cavity or crawlspace, only letting water escape whenever the valve is opened.

Anyone else already thinking about their holiday tablescapes? Because Catherine Zeta-Jones has just given us all the Thanksgiving inspiration we could ever need.

The actor recently shared a glimpse of her and Michael Douglas's Thanksgiving decor, and it's the kind of rustic autumnal display that makes you want to invite everyone over for dinner; think warm orange foliage, miniature pumpkins, natural branches and a gorgeous leafy garland.

It's the same sort of wonderfully unfussy vibe as Michelle Obama's twig tree, and you don't need a celebrity-sized decorating budget to recreate the look. In fact, I'd argue that some of the prettiest ingredients might already be growing in your backyard.

Catherine Zeta-Jones is one of those stars attached to countless big projects, from Wednesday to Chicago to America's Sweethearts. Still, though, she remains wonderfully down-to-earth... and even takes the time to make her own fall decor, too!

'A little DIY in anticipation of Thanksgiving,' she captioned a photo of her table on Instagram. 'I love this up coming holiday, my kids are home from college and I can’t wait!!!'

A post shared by Catherine Zeta-Jones (@catherinezetajones)

Keen to give it a go for yourself? Well, it's easy enough; all you really need to focus on is bringing the beauty of your autumnal garden indoors.

First things first, head outside and gather a selection of autumn leaves in warm shades of orange, red, bronze and gold. Maple and oak leaves are particularly lovely, but don't overlook interesting branches and seasonal greenery, either.

Make like Catherine Zeta-Jones and try using a mixture of different leaf shapes and sizes because it gives the arrangement a more natural, gathered-from-the-garden feel. Then, you can lay the foliage directly along the middle of the table, creating a loose runner that you can build the rest of your decorations around.

Something like the Oasis Forage Floral Create Kit on Amazon could help with this.

This clever little foraging kit has everything you need to get started on crafting your own fall decorations.

Whatever you do, just make sure anything you collect is clean and free from pests. And if you're gathering from outside your garden, always check that you're allowed to collect it.

You can't have a Thanksgiving centerpiece without pumpkins, can you? And Catherine Zeta-Jones's rustic look is a lovely reminder that you don't need enormous pumpkins to make an impact.

I'd choose a mixture of orange, cream and green varieties, placing them at intervals along the foliage. Try grouping a few together rather than spacing everything out too evenly. That slightly imperfect arrangement is what makes the whole thing feel so charming.

If you've grown your own ornamental gourds, even better! They're a wonderful way to give your Thanksgiving decorations a personal touch.

Now for my favorite part: the finishing touches! Honestly, a few interesting branches, seedheads or pinecones will add height and texture to the arrangement, and I particularly love the idea of incorporating dried ornamental grasses, which bring movement and a lovely natural softness to the display.

Then, make like Catherine Zeta-Jones and add small votive candles or LED tealights between the pumpkins and foliage. The warm glow will make the whole table feel wonderfully inviting once the evening draws in.

What I love about Catherine Zeta Jones's rustic decorations is that they remind us how much beauty there is to be found in the changing seasons!

#7935. A Stylish Indoor Herb Garden With Nearly Zero Effort: An Auk Mini 2 Review

Published Oct 30, 2026 8:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

I was already a fan of the original Auk Mini after testing it for our guide to the best grow lights, so I was curious whether the new Auk Mini 2 actually improved on it or simply gave it a facelift. I tested the Espresso/Walnut model on the same kitchen counter where I used the original: an area that receives virtually no natural light. That meant the plants were entirely dependent on the Mini 2’s built-in grow light. I planted all four included pots with the supplied seeds, two basil and two parsley, and grew them for about a month.

The biggest change I noticed right away was the design. The original Auk Mini was already one of the best-looking growing systems I’d tested, but the Mini 2 feels more finished. Its corners are rounder, the transitions between components are smoother, and the whole thing has a more organic shape. I tested the Espresso/Walnut finish again, and it’s still my favorite. The pots have changed, too. Their bottoms are more rounded and extend farther into the reservoir, which appears to give the growing medium better access to water.

Setup is still wonderfully simple. Auk gives you exactly enough prehydrated coco coir for the four pots, and I’ve yet to use another coco coir product that’s as pleasant to work with straight out of the bag. I filled the pots, planted the supplied basil and parsley seeds, scattered the included (and new) small stones over the growing medium, added water and nutrients, and installed the light. That was basically it. The new top layer might seem like a minor addition, but germination and early growth seemed noticeably quicker than with my original Mini. Auk claims the Mini 2 produces 20 percent more growth, and while I didn’t conduct a controlled comparison, my experience certainly supports the idea that plants establish faster in this version.

After roughly a month, all four plants had grown into full, healthy herbs that I was able to harvest for cooking. That’s particularly impressive considering they received no sunlight whatsoever. I didn’t encounter algae, mold, or other growing problems during testing. Maintenance was minimal, too. During the first month as the plants were establishing, I didn’t need to refill the water reservoir.

Once the herbs became established and started drinking more, I simply topped off the reservoir as necessary. At that point, trimming the herbs to keep their growth under control actually became more work than maintaining the garden itself, and that’s hardly a complaint when the payoff is fresh basil and parsley whenever I want them.

There are other upgrades, including an optional app, a new Slow Mode, a larger reservoir, and optional pots designed for larger plants. Those additions make the Mini 2 more versatile, but I don’t think existing Auk Mini owners need to rush out and replace their current unit. The original is still really well made. My biggest complaint is that at $249, I wish Auk included the two larger pots and longer dowels rather than charging another $79 for them. Still, for someone buying their first Auk, I’d absolutely choose the Auk Mini 2. It’s super easy to use, grows plants effectively with minimal effort, and actually looks good while doing it.
